Not extending the sign in the upward and downward directions, but extending it across, he perceives the world as finite in the upward and downward directions, and infinite across.

The rationalist doctrine (takkīvādo) should be understood by the method already stated (vuttanayeneva veditabbo).

These four theorists are included among the speculators about the past (pūrvāntakalpikā) because they apprehend their view as a consequence of what was previously seen by themselves (attanā diṭṭhapubbānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā).
56
56. ‘‘Tatiye ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha antānantikā antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya padhānamanvāya anuyogamanvāya appamādamanvāya sammāmanasikāramanvāya tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte uddhamadho antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. ‘‘So evamāha – ‘antavā ca ayaṃ loko ananto ca. Ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘‘antavā ayaṃ loko parivaṭumo’’ti, tesaṃ musā. Yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘‘ananto ayaṃ loko apariyanto’’ti, tesampi musā. Antavā ca ayaṃ loko ananto ca. Taṃ kissa hetu? Ahañhi ātappamanvāya padhānamanvāya anuyogamanvāya appamādamanvāya sammāmanasikāramanvāya tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusāmi, yathāsamāhite citte uddhamadho antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharāmi, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. Imināmahaṃ etaṃ jānāmi – yathā antavā ca ayaṃ loko ananto cā’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā antānantikā antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti.
56.

Furthermore, venerable ascetics and Brahmins, based on what, relying on what, do [some] propound the world as both finite and infinite? Here, monks, some ascetic or Brahmin, through ardour, through exertion, through application, through non-negligence, through proper attention, attains such concentration of mind (ceto-samādhi) that, with his mind thus concentrated, he dwells perceiving the world as finite (anta-saññī) upwards and downwards, and as infinite (ananta-saññī) across.

He speaks thus: ‘The world is both finite (antavā) and infinite (ananto).’

Those ascetics and Brahmins who declare, “The world is finite (antavā) and bounded (parivaṭumo),” speak falsely.

And those ascetics and Brahmins who declare, “The world is infinite (ananto) and unbounded (apariyanto),” also speak falsely.

The world is both finite (antavā) and infinite (ananto).

What is the reason for that? Because I, through ardour, through exertion, through application, through non-negligence, through proper attention, attain such concentration of mind (ceto-samādhi) that, with my mind thus concentrated, I dwell perceiving the world as finite (anta-saññī) upwards and downwards, and as infinite (ananta-saññī) across.

Therefore I know that the world is both finite (antavā) and infinite (ananto).’

This, monks, is the third case, based on which, relying on which, some ascetics and Brahmins propound the world as both finite and infinite.
54-60.Antasaññīlokasmiṃ viharatīti paṭibhāganimittaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ avaḍḍhetvā taṃ – ‘‘loko’’ti gahetvā antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati, cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā vaḍḍhitakasiṇo pana anantasaññī hoti, uddhamadho avaḍḍhetvā pana tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho antasaññī, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. Takkīvādo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ime cattāropi attanā diṭṭhapubbānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.
54-60. Abiding perceiving the world as finite (antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati): Without having extended the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) to the boundaries of the world-sphere (cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ), apprehending it as the "world" (loko), he abides perceiving the world as finite. But he who has extended the kasiṇa-image to the boundaries of the world-sphere perceives the world to be infinite (anantasaññī). Not extending the sign in the upward and downward directions, but extending it across, he perceives the world as finite in the upward and downward directions, and infinite across.

The rationalist doctrine (takkīvādo) should be understood by the method stated (vuttanayeneva veditabbo).

These four theorists are included among the speculators about the past because they apprehend their view as a consequence of what was previously seen by themselves.
57
57. ‘‘Catutthe ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha antānantikā antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā takkī hoti vīmaṃsī. So takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ evamāha – ‘nevāyaṃ loko antavā, na panānanto. Ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘‘antavā ayaṃ loko parivaṭumo’’ti, tesaṃ musā. Yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘‘ananto ayaṃ loko apariyanto’’ti, tesampi musā. Yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘‘antavā ca ayaṃ loko ananto cā’’ti, tesampi musā. Nevāyaṃ loko antavā , na panānanto’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave , catutthaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā antānantikā antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti.
57. “And in the fourth case, owing to what, with reference to what, are some honorable śramaṇas (samaṇa) and brāhmaṇas (brāhmaṇa) extensionists, proclaiming the world (loka) to be finite (antavat) or infinite (ananta)? Here, bhikkhus, some śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa is a reasoner, an investigator.

He declares his view—hammered out by reason, deduced from his investigations, following his own flight of thought—thus: ‘This world is neither finite nor infinite.’

Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who declare the world to be finite and bounded speak falsely;

and those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who declare the world to be infinite and boundless also speak falsely.

and those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who declare it to be both finite and infinite—all these speak falsely.

This world is neither finite nor infinite.”

This, bhikkhus, is the fourth case, owing to which, with reference to which, some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are extensionists, proclaiming the world to be finite or infinite.
54-60.Antasaññīlokasmiṃ viharatīti paṭibhāganimittaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ avaḍḍhetvā taṃ – ‘‘loko’’ti gahetvā antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati, cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā vaḍḍhitakasiṇo pana anantasaññī hoti, uddhamadho avaḍḍhetvā pana tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho antasaññī, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. Takkīvādo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ime cattāropi attanā diṭṭhapubbānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.
54-60. Abiding perceiving the world as finite ( antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati), means not extending the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimittaṃ) to the boundary of the world-sphere (cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ), apprehending it as the world. He abides perceiving the world as finite. But he who has extended the kasiṇa-image (vaḍḍhitakasiṇo) to the boundary of the world-sphere perceives the world to be infinite (anantasaññī). Not extending the sign in the upward and downward directions, but extending it across, he perceives the world as finite in the upward and downward directions, and infinite across.

The rationalist doctrine (takkīvādo) should be understood by the method already stated (vuttanayeneva veditabbo).

These four theorists are included among the speculators about the past (pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā) because they apprehend their view as a consequence of what was previously seen by themselves.
58
58. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā antānantikā antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā antānantikā antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti, sabbe te imeheva catūhi vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena; natthi ito bahiddhā.
58. "It is on these four grounds, bhikkhus, that those ascetics and Brahmins who are Finitists and Infinitists ( antānantikā), proclaim the world to be finite or infinite (antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi).

Whatever ascetics or Brahmins there may be who proclaim the world to be finite or infinite, all of them do so on these four grounds or on a certain one of them. Outside of these there is none.
54-60.Antasaññīlokasmiṃ viharatīti paṭibhāganimittaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ avaḍḍhetvā taṃ – ‘‘loko’’ti gahetvā antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati, cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā vaḍḍhitakasiṇo pana anantasaññī hoti, uddhamadho avaḍḍhetvā pana tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho antasaññī, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. Takkīvādo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ime cattāropi attanā diṭṭhapubbānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.
54-60. Abiding perceiving the world as finite, [is when] without having extended the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) to the boundaries of the world-sphere (cakkavāḷa-pariyanta), apprehending it as the world (loka), he abides perceiving the world as finite (anta-saññī). But he who has extended the kasiṇa-image to the boundaries of the world-sphere (cakkavāḷa-pariyanta) perceives the world to be infinite (ananta-saññī). Not extending the sign in the upward and downward directions, but extending it across, he perceives the world as finite (anta-saññī) in the upward and downward directions, and infinite (ananta-saññī) across.

The rationalist doctrine (takkī-vāda) should be understood by the method stated.

These four theorists are included among the speculators about the past (pubbantakappikesu), because they apprehend their view as a consequence of what was previously seen by themselves.
59
59. ‘‘Tayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānāti – ‘ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃgahitā evaṃparāmaṭṭhā evaṃgatikā bhavanti evaṃabhisamparāyā’ti. Tañca tathāgato pajānāti, tato ca uttaritaraṃ pajānāti, tañca pajānanaṃ na parāmasati, aparāmasato cassa paccattaññeva nibbuti viditā. Vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto, bhikkhave, tathāgato.
59. "This, monks, the Tathāgata (thus-gone one) understands: 'These viewpoints, thus grasped and thus adhered to, lead to such and such destinations in another life.' (ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃgahitā evaṃparāmaṭṭhā evaṃgatikā bhavanti evaṃabhisamparāyā’ti)
The Tathāgata (thus-gone one) understands this, and even more than this; however, he does not cling to that understanding. Because of this non-clinging, he has realized nirvāṇa (extinguishment) within himself.
Having truly understood the arising (samudaya) and passing away (atthaṅgama), the attraction (assāda) and peril (ādīnava), and the deliverance (nissaraṇa) from feelings (vedanānaṃ) as they really are, the Tathāgata (thus-gone one), monks, is liberated through non-clinging (anupādāvimutto).
54-60.Antasaññīlokasmiṃ viharatīti paṭibhāganimittaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ avaḍḍhetvā taṃ – ‘‘loko’’ti gahetvā antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati, cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā vaḍḍhitakasiṇo pana anantasaññī hoti, uddhamadho avaḍḍhetvā pana tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho antasaññī, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. Takkīvādo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ime cattāropi attanā diṭṭhapubbānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.
54-60. Abiding perceiving the world as finite, means without having extended the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimittaṃ) to the boundary of the world-sphere (cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ), apprehending it as the world, he abides perceiving the world as finite. But he who has extended the kasiṇa-image, that has been increased, to the boundary of the world-sphere perceives the world to be infinite (anantasaññī). Not extending the sign in the upward and downward directions, but extending it across, he perceives the world as finite in the upward and downward directions, and infinite across.

The rationalist doctrine (takkīvādo) should be understood by the method already stated.

These four theorists are included among the speculators about the past because they apprehend their view as a consequence of what was previously seen by themselves.
60
60. ‘‘Ime kho te, bhikkhave, dhammā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā santā paṇītā atakkāvacarā nipuṇā paṇḍitavedanīyā, ye tathāgato sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti, yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
60. "These, monks, are the dharmas that are profound (gambhīrā), difficult to see (duddasā), difficult to understand (duranubodhā), peaceful (santā), excellent (paṇītā), beyond the sphere of reasoning (atakkāvacarā), subtle (nipuṇā), and comprehensible only to the wise (paṇḍitavedanīyā), which the Tathāgata, having realized for himself with direct knowledge (abhiññā sacchikatvā), proclaims (pavedeti); and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality (yathābhuccaṃ) would speak.
54-60.Antasaññīlokasmiṃ viharatīti paṭibhāganimittaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ avaḍḍhetvā taṃ – ‘‘loko’’ti gahetvā antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati, cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā vaḍḍhitakasiṇo pana anantasaññī hoti, uddhamadho avaḍḍhetvā pana tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho antasaññī, tiriyaṃ anantasaññī. Takkīvādo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ime cattāropi attanā diṭṭhapubbānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.
54-60. Abiding perceiving the world as finite (antasaññī lokasmiṃ viharati): Without having extended the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) to the boundaries of the world-sphere (cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ), apprehending it as the world, he abides perceiving the world as finite. But he who has extended the kasiṇa-image to the boundaries of the world-sphere perceives the world to be infinite (anantasaññī). Not extending the sign in the upward and downward directions, but extending it across, he perceives the world as finite in the upward and downward directions, and infinite across.

The rationalist doctrine (takkīvādo) should be understood by the method stated.

These four theorists are included among the speculators about the past because they apprehend their view as a consequence of what was previously seen by themselves.
61
61. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā amarāvikkhepikā, tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ catūhi vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ catūhi vatthūhi?
61. "There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins who are endless equivocators (amarāvikkhepikā). When asked about this or that matter, they resort to evasive statements (vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti) and to endless equivocation (amarāvikkhepaṃ) on four grounds (catūhi vatthūhi).
And owing to what, with reference to what, do these honourable ascetics and Brahmins, who are endless equivocators (amarāvikkhepikā), when asked about this or that matter, resort to evasive statements (vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti) and to endless equivocation (amarāvikkhepaṃ) on four grounds (catūhi vatthūhi)?
61. Na maratīti amarā. Kā sā? Evantipi me notiādinā nayena pariyantarahitā diṭṭhigatikassa diṭṭhi ceva vācā ca. Vividho khepoti vikkhepo, amarāya diṭṭhiyā vācāya ca vikkhepoti amarāvikkhepo, so etesaṃ atthīti amarāvikkhepikā, aparo nayo – amarā nāma ekā macchajāti, sā ummujjananimujjanādivasena udake sandhāvamānā gahetuṃ na sakkāti, evameva ayampi vādo itocito ca sandhāvati, gāhaṃ na upagacchatīti amarāvikkhepoti vuccati. So etesaṃ atthīti amarāvikkhepikā.
61. Na maratīti amarā. "It does not die, thus it is amarā (undying/immortal)."

What is that? It is the view and speech of one whose views are endless (pariyantarahitā) in the manner of "yes" and "no," etc.

"Tossing back and forth in diverse ways" is vikkhepo (equivocation). "Amarāya diṭṭhiyā vācāya ca vikkhepo (equivocation through endless views and speech)" is amarāvikkhepo (endless equivocation). So etesaṃ atthīti amarāvikkhepikā (it belongs to them, thus they are endless equivocators). Another method: amarā is the name of a kind of fish. Because they roam about in the water diving in and out, it is impossible to catch hold of them. Analogously, this doctrine roams about here and there and is impossible to catch hold of, therefore it is called amarāvikkhepo (eel-wriggling).

So etesaṃ atthīti amarāvikkhepikā (therefore it is called "eel-wriggling").
62
62. ‘‘Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ‘idaṃ kusala’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, ‘idaṃ akusala’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmi, ‘‘idaṃ akusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmi. Ahañce kho pana ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto, ‘‘idaṃ akusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto, ‘idaṃ kusala’nti vā byākareyyaṃ, ‘idaṃ akusala’nti vā byākareyyaṃ, taṃ mamassa musā. Yaṃ mamassa musā , so mamassa vighāto. Yo mamassa vighāto so mamassa antarāyo’ti. Iti so musāvādabhayā musāvādaparijegucchā nevidaṃ kusalanti byākaroti, na panidaṃ akusalanti byākaroti, tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjati amarāvikkhepaṃ – ‘evantipi me no; tathātipi me no; aññathātipi me no; notipi me no; no notipi me no’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ.
62.

“Here, bhikkhus, a certain samaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not truly understand what is kusala (wholesome) and what is akusala (unwholesome).

He thinks: ‘I do not truly know what is kusala (wholesome) and what is akusala (unwholesome).'

If, without truly understanding what is kusala (wholesome) and what is akusala (unwholesome), I were to declare something as "kusala (wholesome)" or "akusala (unwholesome)," that would be a lie for me.

If it were a lie for me, that would be distressing for me.

If that were distressing for me, that would be an obstacle for me."

Thus, out of fear of lying and loathing of lying, he does not declare anything to be kusala (wholesome) or akusala (unwholesome). But when questioned about this or that matter, he resorts to evasive statements and endless equivocation: "I don’t say this, I don’t say that. I don’t say it is otherwise. I don’t say it is not. I don’t not say it is not."

This, bhikkhus, is the first basis, resorting to which and on account of which, some samaṇas and brāhmaṇas are eel-wrigglers, and when questioned about this or that matter, they resort to evasive statements and endless equivocation.
62.‘‘Idaṃkusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti dasa kusalakammapathe yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti attho. Akusalepi dasa akusalakammapathāva adhippetā. So mamassa vighātoti ‘‘musā mayā bhaṇita’’nti vippaṭisāruppattiyā mama vighāto assa, dukkhaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. So mamassa antarāyoti so mama saggassa ceva maggassa ca antarāyo assa. Musāvādabhayā musāvādaparijegucchāti musāvāde ottappena ceva hiriyā ca. Vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjatīti vācāya vikkhepaṃ āpajjati. Kīdisaṃ? Amarāvikkhepaṃ, apariyantavikkhepanti attho. Evantipi me notiādīsu evantipi me noti aniyamitavikkhepo . Tathātipi me noti ‘‘sassato attā ca loko cā’’ti vuttaṃ sassatavādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Aññathātipi me noti sassatato aññathā vuttaṃ ekaccasassataṃ paṭikkhipati. Notipi me noti – ‘‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’’ti vuttaṃ ucchedaṃ paṭikkhipati. No notipi me noti ‘‘neva hoti na na hotī’’ti vuttaṃ takkīvādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Sayaṃ pana ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti vā ‘‘akusala’’nti vā puṭṭho na kiñci byākaroti. ‘‘Idaṃ kusala’’nti puṭṭho ‘‘evantipi me no’’ti vadati. Tato ‘‘kiṃ akusala’’nti vutte ‘‘tathātipi me no’’ti vadati. ‘‘Kiṃ ubhayato aññathā’’ti vutte ‘‘aññathātipi me no’’ti vadati. Tato ‘‘tividhenāpi na hoti, kiṃ te laddhī’’ti vutte ‘‘notipi me no’’ti vadati. Tato ‘‘kiṃ no noti te laddhī’’ti vutte ‘‘no notipi me no’’ti evaṃ vikkhepameva āpajjati, ekasmimpi pakkhe na tiṭṭhati.
62. He does not understand as they really are, thus: “This is wholesome ( idaṃ kusala)” which refers to not understanding as they really are the ten courses of wholesome action ( dasa kusalakammapatha), this is the meaning.
And unwholesome (akusala) actions also, the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusalakammapatha) are intended.
“That would distress me”: it might distress me by producing remorse (vippaṭisāru) over having spoken falsely ( musā). The meaning is that it would be painful ( dukkhaṃ).
“That distress would be an obstacle for me”: i. e., an obstacle to attaining heaven (sagga) or the path ( magga).
“Out of fear and loathing of making a false statement (musāvāda)”: due to moral dread (ottappa) and shame (hirī).
He resorts to equivocation ( vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjati), that is, he equivocates in his speech.
What kind of equivocation? Endless (apariyanta) equivocation, that is the meaning.
“I do not take it thus (evantipi me no)” : this is indeterminate equivocation (aniyamitavikkhepo).
“I do not take it in that way (tathātipi me no)” : he rejects the eternalist doctrine (sassatavāda) that the self ( attā) and the world (loka) are eternal ( sassato).
“Nor do I take it in some other way (aññathātipi me no)” : i. e., in some way other than eternalism; by this he rejects partial-eternalism (ekaccasassataṃ).
“I do not say that it is not (notipi me no)” : he rejects the annihilationist doctrine (ucchedaṃ) that “the Tathāgata does not exist after death ( na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā)”.
“Nor do I say that it is neither this nor that (no notipi me no)” : he rejects the rationalist doctrine (takkīvādaṃ) that “the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist ( neva hoti na na hotī) after death.”
When asked, he does not himself declare anything as wholesome (kusala) or unwholesome (akusala) ( sayaṃ pana ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti vā ‘‘akusala’’nti vā puṭṭho na kiñci byākaroti).
When asked: “Is this wholesome (idaṃ kusala)”, he says: “I do not take it thus (evantipi me no)”.
Asked: “What, is it then unwholesome (akusala)?”, he says: “I do not take it that way (tathātipi me no)”.
Asked: “Is it then something other than these two (kiṃ ubhayato aññathā)?”, he says: “Nor do I take it in some other way (aññathātipi me no)”.
Asked: “If it is neither of these three, what is your opinion ( kiṃ te laddhī)?”, he says: “I do not say that it is not (notipi me no)”.
Asked: “In your opinion is it neither this nor that ( kiṃ no noti te laddhī)?”, he says: “Nor do I say that it is neither this nor that ( no notipi me no).” Thus he resorts to equivocation ( vikkhepameva āpajjati) and does not take a stand on any single side ( ekasmimpi pakkhe na tiṭṭhati).
63
63. ‘‘Dutiye ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ‘idaṃ kusala’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, ‘idaṃ akusala’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmi, ‘‘idaṃ akusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmi. Ahañce kho pana ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto, ‘‘idaṃ akusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto, ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti vā byākareyyaṃ, ‘‘idaṃ akusala’nti vā byākareyyaṃ, tattha me assa chando vā rāgo vā doso vā paṭigho vā. Yattha yo (?) me assa chando vā rāgo vā doso vā paṭigho vā, taṃ mamassa upādānaṃ. Yaṃ mamassa upādānaṃ, so mamassa vighāto. Yo mamassa vighāto, so mamassa antarāyo’ti. Iti so upādānabhayā upādānaparijegucchā nevidaṃ kusalanti byākaroti, na panidaṃ akusalanti byākaroti, tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjati amarāvikkhepaṃ – ‘evantipi me no; tathātipi me no; aññathātipi me no; notipi me no; no notipi me no’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ.
63. Furthermore, what is the basis and reason for some ascetics and Brahmins, when questioned on various points, to resort to evasive statements and endless equivocation? Here, monks, some ascetic or Brahmin does not truly understand what is wholesome (kusala) or what is unwholesome (akusala).

They think: "I do not truly know what is good (kusala), nor do I truly know what is bad (akusala)."

If, without truly understanding what is wholesome (kusala) or unwholesome (akusala), I were to declare something to be wholesome (kusala) or unwholesome (akusala), desire (chanda), lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), or aversion (paṭigha) might arise in me.

If desire (chanda), lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), or aversion (paṭigha) were to arise in me, that would be my clinging (upādāna).

If there were clinging (upādāna) on my part, that would distress (vighāta) me.

If I were distressed (vighāta), that would be an obstacle (antarāya) for me."

Therefore, out of fear of clinging (upādāna), and loathing of clinging (upādāna), they do not declare anything to be wholesome (kusala) or unwholesome (akusala). When questioned about this or that point, they resort to evasive statements and endless equivocation: "I don’t say it is this; I don’t say it is that; I don’t say it is otherwise; I don’t say it is not; I don’t not say it is not."

Monks, this is the second reason why some ascetics and Brahmins, when questioned on various points, resort to evasive statements and endless equivocation.
63.Chando vā rāgo vāti ajānantopi sahasā kusalameva ‘‘kusala’’nti vatvā akusalameva ‘‘akusala’’nti vatvā mayā asukassa nāma evaṃ byākataṃ, kiṃ taṃ subyākatanti aññe paṇḍite pucchitvā tehi – ‘‘subyākataṃ, bhadramukha, kusalameva tayā kusalaṃ, akusalameva akusalanti byākata’’nti vutte natthi mayā sadiso paṇḍitoti evaṃ me tattha chando vā rāgo vā assāti attho. Ettha ca chando dubbalarāgo, rāgo balavarāgo. Doso vā paṭigho vāti kusalaṃ pana ‘‘akusala’’nti, akusalaṃ vā ‘‘kusala’’nti vatvā aññe paṇḍite pucchitvā tehi – ‘‘dubyākataṃ tayā’’ti vutte ettakampi nāma na jānāmīti tattha me assa doso vā paṭigho vāti attho. Idhāpi doso dubbalakodho, paṭigho balavakodho. Taṃmamassa upādānaṃ, so mamassa vighātoti taṃ chandarāgadvayaṃ mama upādānaṃ assa, dosapaṭighadvayaṃ vighāto. Ubhayampi vā daḷhaggahaṇavasena upādānaṃ , vihananavasena vighāto. Rāgo hi amuñcitukāmatāya ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhāti jalūkā viya. Doso vināsetukāmatāya āsīviso viya. Ubhopi cete santāpakaṭṭhena vihananti yevāti ‘‘upādāna’’nti ca ‘‘vighāto’’ti ca vuttā. Sesaṃ paṭhamavārasadisameva.
63. "Desire and lust might arise in me": Even without understanding, one might hastily declare the wholesome to be "wholesome" and the unwholesome to be "unwholesome." Then afterward, they ask other wise individuals: "I explained thus to so and so. Was my explanation right?" If they should say: "You explained rightly, good sir, you declared the wholesome to be wholesome and the unwholesome to be unwholesome," they might think: "There is no wise person equal to me"—thus "desire and lust might arise in me." This is the meaning.

Here, chanda is weak attachment, rāga is strong attachment.

"Or hatred and aversion might arise in me": If one declares the wholesome to be unwholesome and the unwholesome to be wholesome, and asks wise people about their reply, they will say: "You explained wrongly." Then they will think: "I do not even know this much"—thus "hatred and aversion might arise in me."

Here also, dosa is weak anger, paṭigha is strong anger.

"That would be clinging on my part. Such clinging would distress me..." The pair, desire (chanda) and lust (rāga), would be clinging (upādāna) on my part; the pair, hatred (dosa) and aversion (paṭigha), would cause distress (vighāta).

Or both pairs are clinging (upādāna) because they are forms of holding firmly, and both cause distress (vighāta) because they cause harm.

For lust (rāga) takes hold of the object like a leech, not desiring to let go of it.

And hatred (dosa) takes hold of it like a poisonous snake (āsīvisa), desiring to destroy it.

And both pairs cause distress, in the sense that they are afflicting. Thus they are called both "clinging" (upādāna) and "distress" (vighāta).

The rest is the same as the first time.
64
64. ‘‘Tatiye ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ‘idaṃ kusala’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, ‘idaṃ akusala’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmi, ‘‘idaṃ akusala’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmi. Ahañce kho pana ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto ‘‘idaṃ akusala’’nti yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto ‘‘idaṃ kusala’’nti vā byākareyyaṃ, ‘‘idaṃ akusala’’nti vā byākareyyaṃ. Santi hi kho samaṇabrāhmaṇā paṇḍitā nipuṇā kataparappavādā vālavedhirūpā, te bhindantā vobhindantā (sī. pī.) maññe caranti paññāgatena diṭṭhigatāni, te maṃ tattha samanuyuñjeyyuṃ samanugāheyyuṃ samanubhāseyyuṃ. Ye maṃ tattha samanuyuñjeyyuṃ samanugāheyyuṃ samanubhāseyyuṃ, tesāhaṃ na sampāyeyyaṃ. Yesāhaṃ na sampāyeyyaṃ, so mamassa vighāto. Yo mamassa vighāto, so mamassa antarāyo’ti. Iti so anuyogabhayā anuyogaparijegucchā nevidaṃ kusalanti byākaroti, na panidaṃ akusalanti byākaroti, tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjati amarāvikkhepaṃ – ‘evantipi me no; tathātipi me no; aññathātipi me no; notipi me no; no notipi me no’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ.
64. Furthermore, venerable monks, what is the basis for those ascetics and Brahmins who are eel-wrigglers, who, when questioned on this or that point, resort to evasive statements and to endless equivocation? Here, monks, some ascetic or Brahmin does not truly understand what is kusala (wholesome) and what is akusala (unwholesome).

He thinks: "I do not truly know what is kusala (wholesome) and what is akusala (unwholesome)."

"If, without truly knowing what is kusala (wholesome) and what is akusala (unwholesome), I were to declare: “This is kusala (wholesome),” or “This is akusala (unwholesome),”

Now, there are ascetics and Brahmins who are wise, clever, experienced in controversy, like archers who can split hairs, who go around destroying others’ views with their wisdom, and they might cross-examine me, demanding my reasons and arguing.

If they should cross-examine me, demanding my reasons and arguing, I might not be able to reply.

If I could not reply, that would distress me.

And if I were distressed, that would be an obstacle for me."

Therefore, out of fear and loathing of being cross-examined, he does not declare anything to be kusala (wholesome) or akusala (unwholesome). But, when questioned about this or that point, he resorts to evasive statements and to endless equivocation: "I do not take it thus, nor do I take it in that way, nor do I take it in some other way. I do not say that it is not, nor do I say that it is neither this nor that."

This, monks, is the third basis for those ascetics and Brahmins who are eel-wrigglers, who, when questioned on this or that point, resort to evasive statements and to endless equivocation.
64.Paṇḍitāti paṇḍiccena samannāgatā. Nipuṇāti saṇhasukhumabuddhino sukhumaatthantaraṃ paṭivijjhanasamatthā. Kataparappavādāti viññātaparappavādā ceva parehi saddhiṃ katavādaparicayā ca. Vālavedhirūpāti vālavedhidhanuggahasadisā. Te bhindantā maññeti vālavedhi viya vālaṃ sukhumānipi paresaṃ diṭṭhigatāni attano paññāgatena bhindantā viya carantīti attho. Te maṃ tatthāti te samaṇabrāhmaṇā maṃ tesu kusalākusalesu. Samanuyuñjeyyunti ‘‘kiṃ kusalaṃ, kiṃ akusalanti attano laddhiṃ vadā’’ti laddhiṃ puccheyyuṃ. Samanugāheyyunti ‘‘idaṃ nāmā’’ti vutte ‘‘kena kāraṇena etamatthaṃ gāheyyu’’nti kāraṇaṃ puccheyyuṃ. Samanubhāseyyunti ‘‘iminā nāma kāraṇenā’’ti vutte kāraṇe dosaṃ dassetvā ‘‘na tvaṃ idaṃ jānāsi, idaṃ pana gaṇha, idaṃ vissajjehī’’ti evaṃ samanuyuñjeyyuṃ. Na sampāyeyyanti na sampādeyyaṃ, sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkuṇeyyanti attho. So mamassa vighātoti yaṃ taṃ punappunaṃ vatvāpi asampāyanaṃ nāma, so mama vighāto assa, oṭṭhatālujivhāgalasosanadukkhameva assāti attho. Sesametthāpi paṭhamavārasadisameva.
64. "Paṇḍitā": endowed with intelligence (paṇḍicca).

"Nipuṇā": of refined and subtle intellect (saṇhasukhumabuddhi), capable of penetrating subtle meanings (sukhumaatthantaraṃ paṭivijjhanasamatthā).

"Kataparappavādā": having knowledge of others' doctrines (viññātaparappavādā), and familiar with engaging in discussions with others (parehi saddhiṃ katavādaparicayā ca).

"Vālavedhirūpā": like a skilled archer (vālavedhidhanuggahasadisā).

It means (attho) that those who destroy (bhindantā) are regarded as piercing even subtle hairs (vālaṃ sukhumānipi) with their knowledge (paññāgatena), like a hair-splitting archer (vālavedhi viya), and wander (caranti) destroying the fixed views (diṭṭhigatāni) of others (paresam).

"Te maṃ tatthāti": those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in those wholesome and unwholesome things may question me (maṃ tesu kusalākusalesu).

"Samanuyuñjeyyunti": they might cross-examine me (samanuyuñjeyyuṃ), asking, "What is wholesome ( kusalaṃ)? What is unwholesome (akusalaṃ)? State your opinion (attano laddhiṃ vadā)!" They might inquire about my opinion (laddhiṃ puccheyyuṃ).

"Samanugāheyyunti": they might press me for reason (samanugāheyyuṃ), saying, "This is my opinion (idaṃ nāmā)," and then ask, "For what reason do you hold this (kena kāraṇena etamatthaṃ gāheyyu)?" They might inquire about the reason (kāraṇaṃ puccheyyuṃ).

"Samanubhāseyyunti": they might refute my statements (samanubhāseyyunti), saying, "For this reason (iminā nāma kāraṇenā)," and pointing out errors (dosaṃ dassetvā) in the reason (kāraṇe), examine me thus (evaṃ samanuyuñjeyyuṃ): "You do not understand this (na tvaṃ idaṃ jānāsi). Accept this (idaṃ pana gaṇha). Answer this (idaṃ vissajjehī)!"

"Na sampāyeyyanti": I might not be able to bring it to completion (na sampādeyyaṃ), meaning (attho) that having completed it, I might not be able to explain it (sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkuṇeyyaṃ).

"So mamassa vighātoti": that would be my ruin (so mama vighāto assa), meaning (attho) that what is called incompletion (asampāyanaṃ nāma) even when repeatedly spoken (yaṃ taṃ punappunaṃ vatvāpi), that would be my ruin (so mama vighāto assa), it would only be suffering (dukkhaṃ eva) due to dryness (sosana) of the lips, palate, tongue and throat (oṭṭhatālujivhāgala).

"Sesametthāpi paṭhamavārasadisameva": the rest is the same as the first instance (paṭhamavārasadisameva).
65
65. ‘‘Catutthe ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā mando hoti momūho. So mandattā momūhattā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjati amarāvikkhepaṃ – ‘atthi paro loko’ti iti ce maṃ pucchasi, ‘atthi paro loko’ti iti ce me assa, ‘atthi paro loko’ti iti te naṃ byākareyyaṃ, ‘evantipi me no, tathātipi me no, aññathātipi me no, notipi me no, no notipi me no’ti. ‘Natthi paro loko…pe… ‘atthi ca natthi ca paro loko…pe… ‘nevatthi na natthi paro loko…pe… ‘atthi sattā opapātikā …pe… ‘natthi sattā opapātikā…pe… ‘atthi ca natthi ca sattā opapātikā…pe… ‘nevatthi na natthi sattā opapātikā…pe… ‘atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ sukaṭadukkaṭānaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.) kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko…pe… ‘natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko…pe… ‘atthi ca natthi ca sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko…pe… ‘nevatthi na natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko…pe… ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā…pe… ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā…pe… ‘hoti ca na ca hoti na hoti ca (sī. ka.) tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā…pe… ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti iti ce maṃ pucchasi, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti iti ce me assa, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti iti te naṃ byākareyyaṃ, ‘evantipi me no, tathātipi me no, aññathātipi me no, notipi me no, no notipi me no’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, catutthaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ.
65. Furthermore, monks, on what grounds do some ascetics and Brahmins, being eel-wrigglers, when questioned about this or that point, resort to evasive statements and to endless equivocation? Here, monks, some ascetic or Brahmin is dull and stupid.

Due to his dullness and stupidity, when he is questioned he resorts to evasive statements and wriggles like an eel: “If you ask me whether there is another world—if I thought so, I would say there is another world. But I don’t say so. And I don’t say otherwise. And I don’t say it is not, and I don’t not say it is not.”

“Is there no other world? …” “Is there both another world and no other world? …” “Is there neither another world nor no other world? … “Are there beings spontaneously reborn? … “Are there no beings spontaneously reborn? …” “Are there both beings spontaneously reborn and no beings spontaneously reborn? … “Are there neither beings spontaneously reborn nor no beings spontaneously reborn? …” “Is there fruit and result of good and bad actions? …” “Is there no fruit and result of good and bad actions? …” “Is there both fruit and result of good and bad actions and no fruit and result of good and bad actions? …” “Is there neither fruit and result of good and bad actions nor no fruit and result of good and bad actions? …” “Does the Tathāgata exist after death? …” “Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? …” “Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? …“Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?” If you ask me, ‘Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?’ if I thought so, I would say so. But I don’t say so. And I don’t say otherwise. And I don’t say it is not, and I don’t not say it is not.”

This, monks, is the fourth case where some ascetics and Brahmins, being eel-wrigglers, when questioned about this or that point, resort to evasive statements and to endless equivocation.
65-66.Mandoti mandapañño apaññassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Momūhoti atisammūḷho. Hotitathāgatotiādīsu satto ‘‘tathāgato’’ti adhippeto. Sesamettha uttānameva. Imepi cattāro pubbe pavattadhammānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.
65-66. "Slow" means slow of wisdom; this is a designation for the unwise.

"Bewildered" means utterly confused.

In such expressions as "he is a tathāgata," sattva is intended by "tathāgata."

The rest is evident here.

These four, too, are included among those who speculate about the past, because their view is apprehended in accordance with a dhamma occurring in the past.
66
66. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ catūhi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ , sabbe te imeheva catūhi vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena, natthi ito bahiddhā…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
66. "It is on these grounds, bhikkhus, that those ascetics and brāhmaṇas who are endless equivocators (amarāvikkhepikā) resort to evasive statements (vācāvikkhepaṃ) and to endless equivocation (amarāvikkhepaṃ) when questioned about this or that point.

Whatever ascetics (samaṇā) or brāhmaṇas there may be who are endless equivocators (amarāvikkhepikā), when questioned about this or that matter, resort to evasive statements (vācāvikkhepaṃ) and to endless equivocation (amarāvikkhepaṃ), all of them do so on these four grounds or on a certain one of them. Outside of these there is none... it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak.
65-66.Mandoti mandapañño apaññassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Momūhoti atisammūḷho. Hotitathāgatotiādīsu satto ‘‘tathāgato’’ti adhippeto. Sesamettha uttānameva. Imepi cattāro pubbe pavattadhammānusāreneva diṭṭhiyā gahitattā pubbantakappikesu paviṭṭhā.
65-66. "One with dull wisdom" (mandapañño) means this is just a name for one without wisdom (apaññassa).

"Extremely confused" (atisammūḷho) means "completely bewildered" (momūho).

Among terms beginning with "becomes a tathāgata" (hotitathāgatoti), a being (satto) is intended by "tathāgata."

The rest here is evident.

These four endless equivocators are included among the speculators about the past because they apprehend their view as a consequence of some dhamma occurring in the past.
67
67. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā adhiccasamuppannikā adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti dvīhi vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha adhiccasamuppannikā adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti dvīhi vatthūhi?
67. “There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins who are Chance-Originationists, and who proclaim the chance origin of the self (ātman) and the world on two grounds.

And owing to what, with reference to what, do these honourable ascetics and Brahmins proclaim their views of chance origination concerning the self (ātman) and the world on two grounds?
67. ‘‘Adhiccasamuppanno attā ca loko cā’’ti dassanaṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ. Taṃ etesaṃ atthīti adhiccasamuppannikā. Adhiccasamuppannanti akāraṇasamuppannaṃ.
67. The view that "the self (ātmā) and the world (loka) originate fortuitously ( adhiccasamuppanna)" is adhiccasamuppanna.

That which exists for them is called adhiccasamuppannikā.

"To originate fortuitously (adhiccasamuppanna)" means to originate without a cause (akāraṇasamuppannaṃ).
68
68. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, asaññasattā nāma devā. Saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavanti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ aññataro satto tamhā kāyā cavitvā itthattaṃ āgacchati. Itthattaṃ āgato samāno agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati. Agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno ātappamanvāya padhānamanvāya anuyogamanvāya appamādamanvāya sammāmanasikāramanvāya tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte saññuppādaṃ anussarati, tato paraṃ nānussarati. So evamāha – ‘adhiccasamuppanno attā ca loko ca. Taṃ kissa hetu? Ahañhi pubbe nāhosiṃ, somhi etarahi ahutvā santatāya pariṇato’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā adhiccasamuppannikā adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti.
68. "There are, monks, certain gods called 'non-percipient beings' (asaññasattā nāma devā).

When perception arises in them (saññuppādā), those gods pass away from that realm (kāyā cavanti).

And it can happen, monks, that a being falls from that state (kāyā cavitvā) and arises in this world (itthattaṃ āgacchati).

Having arisen in this world (itthattaṃ āgato), he goes forth from the household life into homelessness (agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati).

Having gone forth from home to homelessness (agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito), by means of effort (ātappa), exertion (padhāna), application (anuyoga), diligence (appamāda), and right attention (sammāmanasikāra), he attains to such a degree of mental concentration (cetosamādhiṃ phusati) that with his mind thus concentrated (yathāsamāhite citte) he recalls the arising of perception (saññuppādaṃ anussarati), but recalls none before that (tato paraṃ nānussarati).

He speaks thus: ‘The self (attā) and the world (loko) originate fortuitously (adhiccasamuppanno).’

What is the reason for that (taṃ kissa hetu)? Because previously I did not exist (pubbe nāhosiṃ), but now I am (etarahi). Not having been, I sprang into continuous being (ahutvā santatāya pariṇato’ti)."

This, monks, is the first ground (paṭhamaṃ ṭhānaṃ) by which some ascetics and Brahmins (samaṇabrāhmaṇā) who hold the theory of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppannikā) propound that the self (attānaṃ) and the world (lokaṃ) originate fortuitously (adhiccasamuppannaṃ).
68-73.Asaññasattāti desanāsīsametaṃ, acittuppādā rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho. Tesaṃ evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ekacco hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya – ‘‘citte dosaṃ passati, citte sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva sabbabhayāni ca honti, alaṃ iminā cittena, acittakabhāvova santo’’ti, evaṃ citte dosaṃ passitvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññasattesu nibbattati, cittamassa cuticittanirodhena idheva nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha pātubhavati. Te tattha yathā nāma jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati. Evameva jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti, jhānavege pana parihīne tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati. Yasmā pana tāya idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati, tasmā ‘‘saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī’’ti vuttaṃ. Santatāyāti santabhāvāya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Takkīvādopi vuttanayeneva veditabboti.
68-73. "Non-percipient beings": this is the heading of the teaching. Because they arise without mind, their individual forms consist of mere materiality, this is the meaning.

Their origin is explained as follows. Someone who has gone forth into a sectarian order practices the preliminary work of meditation on the wind kasiṇa and develops the fourth jhāna. After emerging from the jhāna he sees the fault in mind thus: “When there is mind, one is exposed to the suffering of having one’s hands mutilated, etc., and to all kinds of perils. Enough with mind! The unconscious state alone is peaceful.” Having thus seen the fault in mind, if he passes away without having fallen from his jhāna, he is reborn in the asaññasatta realm. His mind ceases with the cessation of the dying consciousness, and it reverts right there. Only the aggregate of material form manifests there.

Just as an arrow driven by the propulsive force of the bow-string travels through space to a distance exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the string,

in the same way this being, taking rebirth through the propulsive force of the jhāna, remains in that realm for a time exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the jhāna. When the force of the jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of material form disappears there and a rebirth-linking perception (pratisaṃdhi-saññā) arises here.

Because their passing away from the non-percipient realm is discerned through the arising of perception here, it is said: “When perception arises in them, those gods pass away from that plane.”

Santatayā means to continuous existence.

The rest is evident.

The sophist's doctrine, too, should be understood in the manner stated above.
69
69. ‘‘Dutiye ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha adhiccasamuppannikā adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā takkī hoti vīmaṃsī. So takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ evamāha – ‘adhiccasamuppanno attā ca loko cā’ti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yaṃ āgamma yaṃ ārabbha eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā adhiccasamuppannikā adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti.
69. “And furthermore, venerable ascetics and Brahmins, relying on what, depending on what, do the proponents of chance origin declare the self and the world to have arisen by chance? Here, mendicants, some ascetic or Brahmin is a logician, an investigator.

He declares his view—hammered out by reason (takkapariyāhataṃ), deduced from his investigations (vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ), following his own flight of thought (sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ)—thus: ‘The self (attā) and the world (loko) originate fortuitously (adhiccasamuppanno).’

This, mendicants, is the second ground, relying on which, depending on which, some ascetics and Brahmins declare the self and the world to have arisen by chance."
68-73.Asaññasattāti desanāsīsametaṃ, acittuppādā rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho. Tesaṃ evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ekacco hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya – ‘‘citte dosaṃ passati, citte sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva sabbabhayāni ca honti, alaṃ iminā cittena, acittakabhāvova santo’’ti, evaṃ citte dosaṃ passitvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññasattesu nibbattati, cittamassa cuticittanirodhena idheva nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha pātubhavati. Te tattha yathā nāma jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati. Evameva jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti, jhānavege pana parihīne tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati. Yasmā pana tāya idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati, tasmā ‘‘saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī’’ti vuttaṃ. Santatāyāti santabhāvāya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Takkīvādopi vuttanayeneva veditabboti.
68-73. "Non-percipient beings": this is the heading of the teaching. Because they arise without mind (acittuppāda), their individual forms consist of mere materiality (rūpamattakaattabhāva) – this is the meaning.

Their origin is explained as follows. Someone who has gone forth into a sectarian order practices the preliminary work of meditation on the wind kasiṇa and develops the fourth jhāna. After emerging from the jhāna he sees the fault in mind thus: “When there is mind, one is exposed to the suffering of having one’s hands mutilated, etc., and to all kinds of perils. Enough with mind! The unconscious state alone is peaceful.” Having thus seen the fault in mind, if he passes away without having fallen away from the jhāna, he takes rebirth in the non-percipient realms (asaññasatta). His mind ceases with the cessation of the death-consciousness (cuticittanirodha) and reverts right there, only the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) manifests there.

Just as an arrow driven by the propulsive force of the bow-string travels through space to a distance exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the string,

in the same way, this being, taking rebirth through the propulsive force of the jhāna, remains in that realm for a time exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the jhāna. When the force of the jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) disappears there and a rebirth-linking perception (paṭisandhisaññā) arises here.

Because their passing away from the non-percipient realm is discerned through the arising of perception here, it is said: “When perception arises in them, those gods pass away from that plane.”

"Continuous": in the sense of continuous existence (santabhāva).

The rest is evident.

The view of the sophist (takkīvāda) should also be understood in the manner stated before.
70
70. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā adhiccasamuppannikā adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti dvīhi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā adhiccasamuppannikā adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti, sabbe te imeheva dvīhi vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena, natthi ito bahiddhā…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
70. "It is on these two grounds, bhikkhus, that those ascetics and Brahmins who are Chance-Originists (adhiccasamuppannikā) proclaim the self (ātmā) and the world (loka) to originate fortuitously.

Whatever ascetics (śramaṇa) or Brahmins (brāhmaṇa) there may be who proclaim the self (ātmā) and the world (loka) to originate fortuitously, all of them do so on these two grounds or on a certain one of them. Outside of these there is none... and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak.
68-73.Asaññasattāti desanāsīsametaṃ, acittuppādā rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho. Tesaṃ evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ekacco hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya – ‘‘citte dosaṃ passati, citte sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva sabbabhayāni ca honti, alaṃ iminā cittena, acittakabhāvova santo’’ti, evaṃ citte dosaṃ passitvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññasattesu nibbattati, cittamassa cuticittanirodhena idheva nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha pātubhavati. Te tattha yathā nāma jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati. Evameva jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti, jhānavege pana parihīne tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati. Yasmā pana tāya idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati, tasmā ‘‘saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī’’ti vuttaṃ. Santatāyāti santabhāvāya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Takkīvādopi vuttanayeneva veditabboti.
68-73. "Non-percipient beings": this is the heading of the teaching. Because they arise without mind (acittuppādā), their individual forms consist of mere materiality (rūpamattakaattabhāvā): that is the meaning.

Their origin is explained as follows. Someone who has gone forth into a sectarian order practices the preliminary work of meditation on the wind kasiṇa and develops the fourth jhāna. After emerging from the jhāna he sees the fault in mind thus: “When there is mind, one is exposed to the suffering of having one’s hands mutilated, etc., and to all kinds of perils. Enough with mind! The unconscious state alone is peaceful.” Having thus seen the fault in mind, if he passes away without having fallen away from the jhāna, he takes rebirth among the non-percipient beings (asaññasattesu). His mind ceases with the cessation of the death-consciousness, and it is here that it ceases. Only the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) manifests there.

Just as an arrow driven by the propulsive force of the bow-string travels through space (ākāse) to a distance exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the string,

in the same way this being, taking rebirth through the propulsive force of the jhāna, remains in that realm for a time exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the jhāna. When the force of the jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) disappears there and a rebirth-linking perception (paṭisandhisaññā) arises here.

Because their passing away (cuti) from the non-percipient realm is discerned through the arising of perception here, it is said: “When perception (saññā) arises in them, those gods (devā) pass away from that plane.”

"Continuous" means for the sake of continuous existence (santabhāvāya).

The rest is evident.

The debater (takkīvāda) should also be understood in the manner stated.
71
71. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbantakappikā pubbantānudiṭṭhino pubbantaṃ ārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā pubbantakappikā pubbantānudiṭṭhino pubbantamārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti, sabbe te imeheva aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena, natthi ito bahiddhā.
71. “And these, monks, are the eighteen grounds on which those ascetics and Brahmins who are speculators about the past and hold fixed views about the past assert various conceptual theorems referring to the past.

Whatever ascetics or Brahmins are speculators about the past, hold settled views about the past, and assert various conceptual theorems referring to the past, all of them do so on these eighteen grounds or on a certain one of them. Outside of these there is none.
68-73.Asaññasattāti desanāsīsametaṃ, acittuppādā rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho. Tesaṃ evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ekacco hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya – ‘‘citte dosaṃ passati, citte sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva sabbabhayāni ca honti, alaṃ iminā cittena, acittakabhāvova santo’’ti, evaṃ citte dosaṃ passitvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññasattesu nibbattati, cittamassa cuticittanirodhena idheva nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha pātubhavati. Te tattha yathā nāma jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati. Evameva jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti, jhānavege pana parihīne tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati. Yasmā pana tāya idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati, tasmā ‘‘saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī’’ti vuttaṃ. Santatāyāti santabhāvāya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Takkīvādopi vuttanayeneva veditabboti.
68-73.
Asaññasattā ("non-percipient beings"): this is the heading of the teaching. The meaning is that because they arise without mind (acittuppādā), their individual forms consist of mere materiality (rūpamattakaattabhāvā).

Their origin is explained as follows. Someone who has gone forth into a sectarian order practices the preliminary work of meditation on the wind kasiṇa and develops the fourth jhāna. After emerging from the jhāna he sees the fault in mind thus: “When there is mind, one is exposed to the suffering of having one’s hands mutilated, etc., and to all kinds of perils. Enough with mind! The unconscious state alone is peaceful.” Having thus seen the fault in mind, if he passes away without having fallen away from the jhāna, he is reborn in the asaññasatta realm. His mind ceases with the cessation of the dying consciousness, and it reverts right there. Only the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) manifests there.

Just as an arrow driven by the propulsive force of the bowstring travels through space to a distance exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the string,

in the same way this being, taking rebirth through the propulsive force of the jhāna, remains in that realm for a time exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the jhāna. When the force of the jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of material form disappears there and a rebirth-linking perception (paṭisandhisaññā) arises here.

Because their passing away from the non-percipient realm is discerned through the arising of perception here, it is said: “When perception arises in them (saññuppādā), those gods pass away from that plane.”

Santatāyāti means for the sake of continuity (santabhāvāya).

The rest, here, is but clear.

Even the doctrine of logic (takkīvādopi) should be understood in the manner stated above (vuttanayeneva veditabboti).
72
72. ‘‘Tayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānāti – ‘ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃgahitā evaṃparāmaṭṭhā evaṃgatikā bhavanti evaṃabhisamparāyā’ti. Tañca tathāgato pajānāti, tato ca uttaritaraṃ pajānāti, tañca pajānanaṃ na parāmasati, aparāmasato cassa paccattaññeva nibbuti viditā. Vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto, bhikkhave, tathāgato.
72. "This, monks, the tathāgata understands: ‘These viewpoints (dṛṣṭi-sthānāḥ), thus grasped and thus misapprehended, lead to such destinations and such a future state.’

The tathāgata understands this, and even more than this, yet he does not cling to that understanding. Because he is free from clinging, he has realized peace (nirvṛti) within himself.

Having understood as they really are the origination (samudaya), passing away (atthaṅgama), satisfaction (assāda), unsatisfactoriness (ādīnava), and the escape (nissaraṇa) from feelings (vedanānāṃ), the tathāgata, monks, is liberated through non-clinging (anupādāvimutto)."
68-73.Asaññasattāti desanāsīsametaṃ, acittuppādā rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho. Tesaṃ evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ekacco hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya – ‘‘citte dosaṃ passati, citte sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva sabbabhayāni ca honti, alaṃ iminā cittena, acittakabhāvova santo’’ti, evaṃ citte dosaṃ passitvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññasattesu nibbattati, cittamassa cuticittanirodhena idheva nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha pātubhavati. Te tattha yathā nāma jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati. Evameva jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti, jhānavege pana parihīne tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati. Yasmā pana tāya idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati, tasmā ‘‘saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī’’ti vuttaṃ. Santatāyāti santabhāvāya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Takkīvādopi vuttanayeneva veditabboti.
68-73. "Non-percipient beings": this is the heading of the teaching. Because they arise without mind (acittuppādā), their individual forms consist of mere materiality (rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho).

Their origin is explained as follows. Someone who has gone forth into a sectarian order (titthāyatane pabbajitvā) practices the preliminary work of meditation (parikammaṃ katvā) on the wind kasiṇa and develops the fourth jhāna (catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā). After emerging from the jhāna (jhānā vuṭṭhāya) he sees the fault in mind thus: “When there is mind, one is exposed to the suffering of having one’s hands mutilated, etc., and to all kinds of perils. Enough with mind! The unconscious state alone is peaceful.” Having thus seen the fault in mind, if he passes away without having fallen from the jhāna (aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā), he takes rebirth among the non-percipient beings (asaññasattesu nibbattati). His mind ceases with the cessation of the dying consciousness (cuticittanirodhena), and it reverts right there (idheva nivattati); only the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandhamattameva) manifests there (tattha pātubhavati).

Just as an arrow driven by the propulsive force of the bow-string travels through space to a distance exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the string (jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati),

in the same way this being, taking rebirth through the propulsive force of the jhāna (jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā), remains in that realm for a time exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the jhāna (yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti). When the force of the jhāna is exhausted (jhānavege pana parihīne), the aggregate of material form disappears there (tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati) and a rebirth-linking perception arises here (idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati).

Because their passing away (cuti) from the non-percipient realm is discerned through the arising of perception here (idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati), it is said: “When perception arises (saññuppādā) in them, those gods pass away from that plane (tamhā kāyā cavantī).”

"Continuity" means the state of being continuous (santatāyāti santabhāvāya).

The rest is evident (sesamettha uttānameva).

Also the doctrine of sophistry (takkīvādopi) should be understood in the manner stated (vuttanayeneva veditabbo).
73
73. ‘‘Ime kho te, bhikkhave, dhammā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā santā paṇītā atakkāvacarā nipuṇā paṇḍitavedanīyā, ye tathāgato sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti , yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
73. "These, monks, are those dharmas that are profound (gambhīrā), difficult to see (duddasā), difficult to understand (duranubodhā), peaceful (santā), excellent (paṇītā), beyond the sphere of reasoning (atakkāvacarā), subtle (nipuṇā), comprehensible only to the wise (paṇḍitavedanīyā), which the Tathāgata, having realized for himself with direct knowledge (abhiññā sacchikatvā), propounds to others; and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak.
68-73.Asaññasattāti desanāsīsametaṃ, acittuppādā rūpamattakaattabhāvāti attho. Tesaṃ evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ekacco hi titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya – ‘‘citte dosaṃ passati, citte sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva sabbabhayāni ca honti, alaṃ iminā cittena, acittakabhāvova santo’’ti, evaṃ citte dosaṃ passitvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā asaññasattesu nibbattati, cittamassa cuticittanirodhena idheva nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha pātubhavati. Te tattha yathā nāma jiyāvegakkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati. Evameva jhānavegakkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti, jhānavege pana parihīne tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha pana paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati. Yasmā pana tāya idha uppannasaññāya tesaṃ tattha cuti paññāyati, tasmā ‘‘saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī’’ti vuttaṃ. Santatāyāti santabhāvāya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Takkīvādopi vuttanayeneva veditabboti.
68-73.

“Non-percipient beings”: this is the heading of the teaching. Because they arise without mind, their individual forms consist of mere materiality; this is the meaning.

Their origin is explained as follows. Someone who has gone forth into a sectarian order practices the preliminary work of meditation on the wind kasiṇa and develops the fourth jhāna. After emerging from the jhāna he sees the fault in mind thus: “When there is mind, one is exposed to the suffering of having one’s hands mutilated, etc., and to all kinds of perils. Enough with mind! The unconscious state alone is peaceful.” Having thus seen the fault in mind, if he passes away without having fallen away from the jhāna, he is reborn in the non-percipient realm. His mind ceases there with the cessation of the death-consciousness, and only the aggregate of material form manifests there.

Just as an arrow driven by the propulsive force of the bowstring travels through space to a distance exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the string,

in the same way this being, taking rebirth through the propulsive force of the jhāna, remains in that realm for a time exactly proportional to the propulsive force of the jhāna. When the force of the jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of material form disappears there and a rebirth-linking perception (pratisaṃdhi-saṃjñā) arises here.

Because their passing away from the non-percipient realm is discerned through the arising of perception here, it is said: “When perception arises in them, those gods pass away from that plane.”

Santatāyāti means to the state of continuousness.

The rest is evident.

The argument based on reasoning ( takkīvāda ) should be understood just as has been said.
74
74. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā aparantakappikā aparantānudiṭṭhino, aparantaṃ ārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti catucattārīsāya catucattālīsāya (syā. kaṃ.) vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha aparantakappikā aparantānudiṭṭhino aparantaṃ ārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti catucattārīsāya vatthūhi?
74. "There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins who are speculators about the future, who hold settled views about the future, and who, with reference to the future, assert various conceptual theorems in forty-four ways, on forty-four grounds.

And owing to what, with reference to what, do these honorable ascetics and Brahmins frame their speculations about the future, holding fixed views about the future, and assert various conceptual theorems concerning the future in forty-four ways?
74. Evaṃ aṭṭhārasa pubbantakappike dassetvā idāni catucattārīsaṃ aparantakappike dassetuṃ – ‘‘santi, bhikkhave’’tiādimāha. Tattha anāgatakoṭṭhāsasaṅkhātaṃ aparantaṃ kappetvā gaṇhantīti aparantakappikā, aparantakappo vā etesaṃ atthīti aparantakappikā. Evaṃ sesampi pubbe vuttappakāranayeneva veditabbaṃ.
74. Having shown the eighteen kinds of speculation about the past ( pubbantakappike ) in this way, now, in order to show the forty-four kinds of speculation about the future ( aparantakappike ), he said, "There are, monks," etc.

There, those who speculate and grasp the future, which is reckoned as the future portion, are aparantakappikā, or these have speculation about the future, therefore, aparantakappikā.

Thus, the rest should also be understood in the same way as previously stated.
75
75. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā uddhamāghātanikā saññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ saññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti soḷasahi vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha uddhamāghātanikā saññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ saññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti soḷasahi vatthūhi?
75. "Monks, there are some ascetics and Brahmins who are proponents of the doctrine of conscious survival after death. They propound that the self is conscious after death based on sixteen grounds.

And upon what grounds, based on what, do these venerable ascetics and Brahmins, who are proponents of the doctrine of conscious survival after death, propound that the self is conscious after death based on sixteen grounds?
75.Uddhamāghātanikāti āghātanaṃ vuccati maraṇaṃ, uddhamāghātanā attānaṃ vadantīti uddhamāghātanikā. Saññīti pavatto vādo, saññīvādo, so etesaṃ atthīti saññīvādā.
75. Uddhamāghātanikā: āghātanaṃ is said to be death (maraṇaṃ); those who speak of self-destruction (attānaṃ vadanti) are uddhamāghātanikā.

Saññīti pavatto vādo, saññīvādo: a discourse (vādo) that proceeds with perception (saññī), is saññīvādo; those who have that are saññīvādā.
76
76. ‘‘‘Rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī’ti naṃ paññapenti. ‘Arūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī’ti naṃ paññapenti. ‘Rūpī ca arūpī ca attā hoti…pe… nevarūpī nārūpī attā hoti… antavā attā hoti… anantavā attā hoti… antavā ca anantavā ca attā hoti… nevantavā nānantavā attā hoti… ekattasaññī attā hoti… nānattasaññī attā hoti… parittasaññī attā hoti… appamāṇasaññī attā hoti… ekantasukhī attā hoti… ekantadukkhī attā hoti. Sukhadukkhī attā hoti. Adukkhamasukhī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī’ti naṃ paññapenti.
76. They declare that the self after death is healthy, conscious, and: material (rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī).
They declare that the self after death is healthy, conscious, and: immaterial (arūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī).
The self is both material and immaterial, neither material nor immaterial, finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, neither finite nor infinite, of uniform perception, of diversified perception, of limited perception, of boundless perception, exclusively happy, exclusively miserable.
The self is both happy and miserable (sukhadukkhī attā hoti).
They declare that the self after death is healthy, conscious, and: neither happy nor miserable (adukkhamasukhī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī).
76-77.Rūpī attātiādīsu kasiṇarūpaṃ ‘‘attā’’ti tattha pavattasaññañcassa ‘‘saññā’’ti gahetvā vā ājīvakādayo viya takkamatteneva vā ‘‘rūpī attā hoti, arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī’’ti naṃ paññapenti. Tattha arogoti nicco. Arūpasamāpattinimittaṃ pana ‘‘attā’’ti samāpattisaññañcassa ‘‘saññā’’ti gahetvā vā nigaṇṭhādayo viya takkamatteneva vā ‘‘arūpī attā hoti, arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī’’ti naṃ paññapenti. Tatiyā pana missakagāhavasena pavattā diṭṭhi. Catutthā takkagāheneva. Dutiyacatukkaṃ antānantikavāde vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tatiyacatukke samāpannakavasena ekattasaññī , asamāpannakavasena nānattasaññī, parittakasiṇavasena parittasaññī, vipulakasiṇavasena appamāṇasaññīti veditabbā. Catutthacatukke pana dibbena cakkhunā tikacatukkajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘ekantasukhī’’ti gaṇhāti. Niraye nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘ekantadukkhī’’ti. Manussesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘sukhadukkhī’’ti. Vehapphaladevesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘adukkhamasukhī’’ti gaṇhāti. Visesato hi pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇalābhino pubbantakappikā honti, dibbacakkhukā aparantakappikāti.
76-77. Regarding "the self is material" etc., they proclaim, "The self is material, healthy (aroga), and percipient (saññī) after death," either by taking the material form (rūpa) of the kasiṇa object as the self (attā), and its perception (saññā) as the self's perception, or by mere reasoning, as in the case of the Ājīvakas etc. Here, aroga means eternal (nicca).

Moreover, regarding the signs of the immaterial attainments (arūpasamāpatti) as the self (attā), and the perception (saññā) occurring in the attainment as the self's perception, or by mere reasoning as in the case of the Nigaṇṭhas, they proclaim: “The self is immaterial (arūpī), healthy (aroga), and percipient (saññī) after death.”

The third view (diṭṭhi) arises by combining the views.

The fourth [arises] through reasoning (takka) alone.

The second tetrad should be understood in the same way as stated in the discussion of extensionism (antānantikavāda).

In the third tetrad: one should understand that the perception of uniformity (ekattasaññī) is due to attainment (samāpannakavasena); the perception of diversity (nānattasaññī) is due to non-attainment (asamāpannakavasena); the perception of limitation (parittasaññī) is due to a limited kasiṇa (parittakasiṇavasena); and the perception of boundlessness (appamāṇasaññī) is due to an expanded kasiṇa (vipulakasiṇavasena).

In the fourth tetrad, having seen with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā) a being taking rebirth on the plane of the first three or four jhānas, one holds that the self is "exclusively happy" (ekantasukhī).

Having seen a being reborn in hell (niraya), he holds that the self is "exclusively miserable" (ekantadukkhī).

Having seen a being reborn in the human world (manussesu), he holds that the self is "both happy and miserable" (sukhadukkhī).

Having seen a being reborn among the Vehapphala gods, he holds that the self is "neither happy nor miserable" (adukkhamasukhī).

Specifically, those who have gained the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) speculate about the past (pubbantakappikā), while those who have the divine eye (dibbacakkhukā) speculate about the future (aparantakappikā).
77
77. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā uddhamāghātanikā saññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ saññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti soḷasahi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā uddhamāghātanikā saññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ saññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti, sabbe te imeheva soḷasahi vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena, natthi ito bahiddhā…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
77. "It is on these sixteen grounds, monks, that those ascetics and Brahmins who maintain a doctrine of percipient immortality proclaim the self to survive percipient after death.

Whatever ascetics or Brahmins maintain a doctrine of percipient immortality, all of them do so on these sixteen grounds or on a certain one of them. Outside of these there is none… and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak."
76-77.Rūpī attātiādīsu kasiṇarūpaṃ ‘‘attā’’ti tattha pavattasaññañcassa ‘‘saññā’’ti gahetvā vā ājīvakādayo viya takkamatteneva vā ‘‘rūpī attā hoti, arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī’’ti naṃ paññapenti. Tattha arogoti nicco. Arūpasamāpattinimittaṃ pana ‘‘attā’’ti samāpattisaññañcassa ‘‘saññā’’ti gahetvā vā nigaṇṭhādayo viya takkamatteneva vā ‘‘arūpī attā hoti, arogo paraṃ maraṇā saññī’’ti naṃ paññapenti. Tatiyā pana missakagāhavasena pavattā diṭṭhi. Catutthā takkagāheneva. Dutiyacatukkaṃ antānantikavāde vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tatiyacatukke samāpannakavasena ekattasaññī , asamāpannakavasena nānattasaññī, parittakasiṇavasena parittasaññī, vipulakasiṇavasena appamāṇasaññīti veditabbā. Catutthacatukke pana dibbena cakkhunā tikacatukkajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘ekantasukhī’’ti gaṇhāti. Niraye nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘ekantadukkhī’’ti. Manussesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘sukhadukkhī’’ti. Vehapphaladevesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘‘adukkhamasukhī’’ti gaṇhāti. Visesato hi pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇalābhino pubbantakappikā honti, dibbacakkhukā aparantakappikāti.
76-77. Regarding views beginning with "The self is material ( rūpī attā)," some, like the Ājīvakas, proclaim: "The self is material (rūpī attā hoti), immutable after death (arogo paraṃ maraṇā), and percipient (saññī)," either by apprehending the material form (kasiṇarūpaṃ) as the self (attā), and the perception that occurs in that context as "perception" (saññā), or simply through reasoning (takkamattena eva).

Here, "immutable (arogo)" means eternal (nicco).

Regarding the signs (nimittaṃ) of the immaterial attainments (arūpasamāpatti), some, like the Nigaṇṭhas, proclaim: "The self is immaterial (arūpī attā hoti), immutable after death (arogo paraṃ maraṇā), and percipient (saññī)," either by apprehending the signs of the attainment as the self (attā), and the perception that occurs in the attainment as "perception" (saññā), or simply through reasoning (takkamattena eva).

The third view (tatiyā diṭṭhi) arises by way of combining (missakagāhavasena pavattā).

The fourth (catutthā) arises simply through reasoning (takkagāhena eva).

The second tetrad (dutiyacatukkaṃ) should be understood in the manner described in the discussion on extensionism (antānantikavāde).

In the third tetrad (tatiyacatukke): the doctrine that the self is of uniform perception (ekattasaññī) pertains to one who attains the meditative attainments (samāpannakavasena); the doctrine that the self is of diversified perception (nānattasaññī) pertains to the non-attainer (asamāpannakavasena); the doctrine that the self is of limited perception (parittasaññī) pertains to one who employs a limited kasiṇa (parittakasiṇavasena); and the doctrine that the self is of boundless perception (appamāṇasaññī) pertains to one who employs an expanded kasiṇa (vipulakasiṇavasena).

With the fourth tetrad (catutthacatukke), having seen with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā) a being taking rebirth on the plane of the first three or four jhānas (tikacatukkajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbattamānaṃ disvā), he holds that the self is "exclusively happy" (ekantasukhī).

Having seen a being reborn in hell (niraye nibbattamānaṃ disvā), he [holds that the self is] "exclusively miserable" (ekantadukkhī).

Having seen a being reborn in the human world (manussesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā), he [holds that the self is] "both happy and miserable" (sukhadukkhī).

Having seen a being reborn among the Vehapphala gods (vehapphaladevesu nibbattamānaṃ disvā), he [holds that the self is] "neither happy nor miserable" (adukkhamasukhī).

Generally (visesato hi), those who gain the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇalābhino) speculate about the past (pubbantakappikā honti), [and] those who gain the divine eye (dibbacakkhukā) speculate about the future (aparantakappikā).
78
78. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā uddhamāghātanikā asaññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ asaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti aṭṭhahi vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha uddhamāghātanikā asaññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ asaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti aṭṭhahi vatthūhi?
78. “There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins who maintain a doctrine of unconscious survival after death, and they propound that the self survives unconscious after death on eight grounds.

On what grounds, based on what, do those ascetics and Brahmins, maintaining a doctrine of unconscious survival after death, propound that the self survives unconscious after death on eight grounds?
78-83. Asaññīvādo saññīvāde ādimhi vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo. Kevalañhi tattha ‘‘saññī attā’’ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha ‘‘asaññī’’ti ca ‘‘nevasaññīnāsaññī’’ti ca. Tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikassa hi gāho ummattakapacchisadisoti vuttametaṃ.
78-83. The doctrine of non-percipient immortality (asaññī-vāda) should be understood in terms of the first two tetrads of the doctrine of percipient immortality (saññī-vāda).
Likewise, the doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient immortality (nevasaññīnāsaññī-vāda).
Only those theorists held the view there that the self (attā) is percipient (saññī), while these respectively hold that it is non-percipient (asaññī) and neither percipient nor non-percipient (nevasaññīnāsaññī).
No special reason need be sought for this.
For the theorists’ assumptions (diṭṭhi-gatika) are said to be like the basket of a madman (ummattaka-pacchi).
79
79. ‘‘‘Rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā asaññī’ti naṃ paññapenti. ‘Arūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā asaññī’ti naṃ paññapenti. ‘Rūpī ca arūpī ca attā hoti…pe… nevarūpī nārūpī attā hoti… antavā attā hoti… anantavā attā hoti… antavā ca anantavā ca attā hoti… nevantavā nānantavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā asaññī’ti naṃ paññapenti.
79. “They declare: ‘The self is material (rūpī attā) after death, healthy (aroga) and non-percipient (asaññī).’
‘The self is immaterial (arūpī attā) after death, healthy (aroga) and non-percipient (asaññī).’
‘The self is both material and immaterial (rūpī ca arūpī ca attā)…pe…neither material nor immaterial (nevarūpī nārūpī attā)…finite (antavā attā)…infinite (anantavā attā)…both finite and infinite (antavā ca anantavā ca attā)…neither finite nor infinite (nevantavā nānantavā attā) after death, healthy (aroga) and non-percipient (asaññī).”
78-83. Asaññīvādo saññīvāde ādimhi vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo.
