Kevalañhi tattha ‘‘saññī attā’’ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha ‘‘asaññī’’ti ca ‘‘nevasaññīnāsaññī’’ti ca. Tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikassa hi gāho ummattakapacchisadisoti vuttametaṃ.
78-83. The doctrine of non-percipient immortality ( asaññī-vāda) should be understood in terms of the first two tetrads of the doctrine of percipient immortality (saññī-vāda). Similarly, so should the doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient immortality (nevasaññīnāsaññī-vāda). Only those theorists held the view that the self (attā) is percipient (saññī), while these respectively hold that it is non-percipient (asaññī) and neither percipient nor non-percipient (nevasaññīnāsaññī). No special reason (kāraṇa) need be sought for this. For the theorists’ assumptions are like the basket of a madman.
80
80. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā uddhamāghātanikā asaññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ asaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti aṭṭhahi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā uddhamāghātanikā asaññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ asaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti, sabbe te imeheva aṭṭhahi vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena, natthi ito bahiddhā…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
80. "It is on these eight grounds, monks, that those ascetics and Brahmins who maintain a doctrine of non-percipient immortality proclaim the self to survive non-percipient after death.

Whatever ascetics or Brahmins maintain a doctrine of non-percipient immortality, all of them do so on these eight grounds or on a certain one of them. Outside of these there is none... and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak.
78-83. Asaññīvādo saññīvāde ādimhi vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo. Kevalañhi tattha ‘‘saññī attā’’ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha ‘‘asaññī’’ti ca ‘‘nevasaññīnāsaññī’’ti ca. Tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikassa hi gāho ummattakapacchisadisoti vuttametaṃ.
78-83. The doctrine of non-percipient immortality ( asaññīvādo) should be understood in terms of the first two tetrads of the doctrine of percipient immortality ( saññīvāde). And also that of neither percipient nor non-percipient immortality (nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo). Only those theorists held the view that the self (attā) is percipient (saññī), while these respectively hold that it is non-percipient (asaññī) and neither percipient nor non-percipient (nevasaññīnāsaññī). No special reason (kāraṇaṃ) need be sought for this. For the theorists’ assumptions are said to be like the basket of a madman.
81
81. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā uddhamāghātanikā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā, uddhamāghātanaṃ nevasaññīnāsaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti aṭṭhahi vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha uddhamāghātanikā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ nevasaññīnāsaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti aṭṭhahi vatthūhi?
81. “There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins who maintain a doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient post-mortem survival (uddhamāghātanikā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā), and they propound the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient after death on eight grounds.

And upon what, based on what, do those esteemed ascetics and Brahmins, who are proponents of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient post-mortem survival, propound the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient after death on eight grounds?
78-83. Asaññīvādo saññīvāde ādimhi vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo. Kevalañhi tattha ‘‘saññī attā’’ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha ‘‘asaññī’’ti ca ‘‘nevasaññīnāsaññī’’ti ca. Tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikassa hi gāho ummattakapacchisadisoti vuttametaṃ.
78-83. The doctrine of non-percipient immortality ( asaññī-vāda) should be understood in terms of the first two tetrads of the doctrine of percipient immortality (saññī-vāda). Likewise, the doctrine of neither percipient nor non-percipient immortality (nevasaññīnāsaññī-vāda). Indeed, only those theorists held the view that the self (attā) is percipient (saññī), while these respectively hold that it is non-percipient (asaññī) and neither percipient nor non-percipient (nevasaññīnāsaññī). No special reason (kāraṇa) need be sought for this. For the theorists’ assumptions (gāho) are said to be like the basket of a madman (ummattaka-pacchi-sadiso).
82
82. ‘‘‘Rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā nevasaññīnāsaññī’ti naṃ paññapenti ‘arūpī attā hoti…pe… rūpī ca arūpī ca attā hoti… nevarūpī nārūpī attā hoti… antavā attā hoti… anantavā attā hoti… antavā ca anantavā ca attā hoti… nevantavā nānantavā attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā nevasaññīnāsaññī’ti naṃ paññapenti.
82. They propound: 'The self (ātman) is with form (rūpī), healthy (aroga), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), neither conscious nor unconscious (nevasaññīnāsaññī)'. They propound: 'The self is without form (arūpī)…and so on… The self is both with and without form (rūpī ca arūpī ca attā hoti)… The self is neither with nor without form (nevarūpī nārūpī attā hoti)… The self is finite (antavā attā hoti)… The self is infinite (anantavā attā hoti)… The self is both finite and infinite (antavā ca anantavā ca attā hoti)… The self is neither finite nor infinite (nevantavā nānantavā attā hoti), healthy (aroga), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), neither conscious nor unconscious (nevasaññīnāsaññī)'.
78-83. Asaññīvādo saññīvāde ādimhi vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo. Kevalañhi tattha ‘‘saññī attā’’ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha ‘‘asaññī’’ti ca ‘‘nevasaññīnāsaññī’’ti ca. Tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikassa hi gāho ummattakapacchisadisoti vuttametaṃ.
78-83. The doctrine of non-percipient immortality (asaññī-vāda) should be understood in terms of the first two tetrads of the doctrine of percipient immortality (saññī-vāda).
Likewise, the doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient immortality (nevasaññī-nāsaññī-vāda).
Only those theorists hold the view that the self (attā) is percipient (saññī); here, however, it is respectively non-percipient (asaññī), and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient (nevasaññī-nāsaññī).
No special reason need be sought for this.
For the theorists’ assumptions (diṭṭhi-gatika) are said to be like the basket of a madman (ummattaka-pacchi-sadisa).
83
83. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā uddhamāghātanikā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ nevasaññīnāsaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti aṭṭhahi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā uddhamāghātanikā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā uddhamāghātanaṃ nevasaññīnāsaññiṃ attānaṃ paññapenti, sabbe te imeheva aṭṭhahi vatthūhi…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
83. "It is on these eight grounds, monks, that those ascetics and Brahmins who maintain a doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient survival proclaim the self to survive neither percipient nor non-percipient after death.

Whatever ascetics or Brahmins maintain a doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient survival, all of them do so on these eight grounds…and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata (Tathāgata) in accordance with reality would speak.
78-83. Asaññīvādo saññīvāde ādimhi vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo. Kevalañhi tattha ‘‘saññī attā’’ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha ‘‘asaññī’’ti ca ‘‘nevasaññīnāsaññī’’ti ca. Tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikassa hi gāho ummattakapacchisadisoti vuttametaṃ.
78-83. The doctrine of non-percipient immortality (asaññīvādo) should be understood in terms of the first two tetrads of the doctrine of percipient immortality (saññīvāde).

And also that of neither percipient nor non-percipient immortality (nevasaññīnāsaññīvādo).

Only those theorists held the view that the self (attā) is percipient (saññī), while these respectively hold that it is non-percipient (asaññī) and neither percipient nor non-percipient (nevasaññīnāsaññī).

No special reason (kāraṇaṃ) need be sought for this.

For the theorists’ assumptions (gāho) are said to be like the basket of a madman (ummattakapacchisadiso).
84
84. ‘‘Santi , bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā ucchedavādā sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti sattahi vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha ucchedavādā sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti sattahi vatthūhi?
84. "There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins who are annihilationists (ucchedavāda) and who, on seven grounds, proclaim the annihilation (uccheda), destruction (vināsa), and extermination (vibhava) of an existent being (sato sattassa).

And upon what grounds do those ascetics and Brahmins, being annihilationists (ucchedavāda), proclaim the annihilation (uccheda), destruction (vināsa), and extermination (vibhava) of an existent being (sato sattassa) on seven grounds (sattahi vatthūhi)?
84. Ucchedavāde satoti vijjamānassa. Ucchedanti upacchedaṃ . Vināsanti adassanaṃ. Vibhavanti bhāvavigamaṃ. Sabbānetāni aññamaññavevacanāneva. Tattha dve janā ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhanti, lābhī ca alābhī ca. Lābhī arahato dibbena cakkhunā cutiṃ disvā upapattiṃ apassanto, yo vā cutimattameva daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti, na upapātaṃ; so ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Alābhī ca ‘‘ko paralokaṃ na jānātī’’ti kāmasukhagiddhatāya vā. ‘‘Yathā rukkhato paṇṇāni patitāni na puna viruhanti, evameva sattā’’tiādinā takkena vā ucchedaṃ gaṇhāti. Idha pana taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena tathā ca aññathā ca vikappetvāva imā satta diṭṭhiyo uppannāti veditabbā.
84. In the annihilationist doctrine, "being" means existing.
"Cutting off" means interruption.
"Destruction" means non-seeing ( adassanaṃ).
"Disappearance" means the passing away of being.
All these are synonyms for one another.
There, two types of people hold the annihilationist view ( ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhanti), the possessor ( lābhī) and the non-possessor ( alābhī).
The possessor ( lābhī) adopts the annihilationist view ( ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti) when, with the divine eye ( dibbena cakkhunā), he sees the passing away ( cutiṃ disvā) of an arhat without seeing any rebirth ( upapattiṃ apassanto), or when he is only able to perceive the mere passing away ( cutimattameva daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti), and not the rebirth ( na upapātaṃ).
The non-possessor ( alābhī ca) adopts the annihilationist view because he thinks, "Who knows about the next world ( ko paralokaṃ na jānātī)?", or due to his greed for sensual pleasures ( kāmasukhagiddhatāya vā).
Or by way of reasoning, e.g., as follows: “Just as leaves ( paṇṇāni) which fall from a tree ( rukkhato) never grow again ( na puna viruhanti), even so are beings ( evameva sattā)," he grasps at annihilation ( ucchedaṃ gaṇhāti).
Here, however, it should be understood ( veditabbā) that these seven views ( imā satta diṭṭhiyo uppannāti) have arisen on account of craving ( taṇhā) and views ( diṭṭhīnaṃ), in one way ( tathā) or another ( aññathā), or by proceeding eclectically ( vikappetvāva).
85
85. ‘‘Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi evaṃdiṭṭhī (ka. pī.) – ‘yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā rūpī cātumahābhūtiko mātāpettikasambhavo kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.
85. "Here, monks, some renunciate (śramaṇa) or Brahmin asserts the following view and opinion: 'When this self (ātmā), good sir, is material (rūpī), composed of the four great elements (cātumahābhūtika), originating from mother and father (mātāpettikasambhava), at the breaking up (bhedā) of the body (kāya) it is annihilated (ucchijjati) and perishes (vinassati), and does not exist after death (maraṇā). At this point, good sir, the self (ātmā) is completely annihilated (sammā samucchinno)'.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation (uccheda), destruction (vināśa), and extermination (vibhava) of an existent being (sattva)."
85. Tattha rūpīti rūpavā. Cātumahābhūtikoti catumahābhūtamayo. Mātāpitūnaṃ etanti mātāpettikaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Sukkasoṇitaṃ. Mātāpettike sambhūto jātoti mātāpettikasambhavo. Iti rūpakāyasīsena manussattabhāvaṃ ‘‘attā’’ti vadati. Ittheketi itthaṃ eke evameketi attho.
85. There, rūpī means possessing rūpa (form).
Cātumahābhūtika means consisting of the four great elements (catumahābhūta).
Mātāpitūnaṃ etanti mātāpettikaṃ means originating from mother and father, hence mātāpettikaṃ.
What is that? Semen and blood (śukraśoṇita).
Born and produced from mother and father, hence mātāpettikasambhava.
Thus, the first theorist asserts the human form under the heading of the material body, to be the self (ātmā).
Itthā means thus, some [say] thus, some [say] like this, such is the meaning.
86
86. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā dibbo rūpī kāmāvacaro kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkho. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.
86. "To him another says: 'There is, good sir, such a self (ātman) as you assert. I do not deny it. But it is not at that point that the self is completely annihilated.
For there is another self—divine (divya), having material form (rūpin), pertaining to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), feeding on edible nutriment.
That you neither know nor see.
But I know it and see it.
Since this self, good sir, is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, at this point the self is completely annihilated.'
That is how some proclaim the annihilation (uccheda), destruction (vināśa), and nonexistence (vibhava) of beings.
86. Dutiyo taṃ paṭikkhipitvā dibbattabhāvaṃ vadati. Dibboti devaloke sambhūto. Kāmāvacaroti cha kāmāvacaradevapariyāpanno. Kabaḷīkāraṃ āhāraṃ bhakkhatīti kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkho.
86. The second, rejecting this, asserts the state of being divine (dibbattabhāvaṃ).

"Divine" (dibbo) means originating (sambhūto) in the world of the gods (devaloke).

"Pertaining to the sense sphere" (kāmāvacaro) means included among the six classes of sense-sphere gods (cha kāmāvacaradevapariyāpanno).

Because one consumes (bhakkhati) solid food (kabaḷīkāraṃ āhāraṃ), therefore one is an eater of solid food (kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkho).
87
87. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā dibbo rūpī manomayo sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī ahīnindriyo. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.
87. Another says to him: "Sir, there is such a self (ātman) as you say; I do not deny its existence. But that self is not wholly annihilated at that point.
For there is, good sir, another self—divine (divya), having material form (rūpin), mind-made (manomaya), complete in all its limbs and organs (sabvaṅgapaccaṅgin), not destitute of any faculties (ahīnindriya).
That you neither know nor see.
But I know it and see it.
Since this self, good sir, is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, at this point the self is completely annihilated."
That is how some proclaim the annihilation (uccheda), destruction (vināsa), and non-existence (vibhava) of beings.
87.Manomayoti jhānamanena nibbatto. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgīti sabbaṅgapaccaṅgayutto. Ahīnindriyoti paripuṇṇindriyo. Yāni brahmaloke atthi, tesaṃ vasena itaresañca saṇṭhānavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ.
87. "Mind-made" (manomaya) means produced through this jhāna mind.
"Possessing all limbs and secondary limbs" (sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī) means endowed with all limbs and secondary limbs.
“Not destitute of any faculties” (ahīnindriya) means complete in its faculties (paripuṇṇindriya).
This is said by way of the faculties that exist in the Brahma-world and by way of the figures of the others.
88
88. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho , bho, añño attā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘‘ananto ākāso’’ti ākāsānañcāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.
88. Another says to him: ‘Good sir, there is a self (ātman) such as you describe, I do not deny that it exists; however, it is not at this point that the self is completely annihilated (sammā samucchinno hoti).

For there is, good sir, another self (ātman) belonging to the base of infinite space, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form (rūpasaññānaṃ), by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance (paṭighasaññānaṃ), by non-attention to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññānaṃ), thinking "space is infinite" (ananto ākāso), one attains to the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatanūpago).

You neither know nor see that.

But I know and see it.

It is this self (ātman) that at the breaking-up of the body (kāyassa bhedā) is annihilated (ucchijjati) and perishes (vinassati), and does not exist after death (paraṃ maraṇā). It is in this way that the self (ātman) is completely annihilated (sammā samucchinno hoti.’

In this way some proclaim the annihilation (ucchedaṃ), destruction (vināsaṃ), and extermination (vibhavaṃ) of an existent being (sato sattassa).
88-92.Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagotiādīsu pana ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaṃ upagatoti, evamattho veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.
88-92. The meaning of "utterly transcending all perceptions of form," and so on, is explained in the Visuddhimagga.

Furthermore, regarding "having attained the sphere of infinite space," and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: "he has attained the state of the sphere of infinite space."

The rest, here, is but clear.
89
89. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.
89. Another one says to him: 'Good sir, there is a self (ātmā) as you say. I do not deny it. However, that self is not completely annihilated at that point.
There is another self (ātmā) which, by entirely surpassing the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ), and [realizing] that "consciousness (vijñāṇa) is infinite" has attained the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ).
That you neither know nor see.
But I know it and see it.
It is this self (ātmā), good sir, that is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body (kāyassa bhedā) and does not exist after death (maraṇā). At this point, the self (ātmā) is completely annihilated.'
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation (ucchedaṃ), destruction (vināsaṃ), and non-existence (vibhavaṃ) of an existent being.
88-92.Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagotiādīsu pana ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaṃ upagatoti, evamattho veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.
88-92. The meaning of "utterly transcending all perceptions of form," and so on, is explained in the Visuddhimagga.

Furthermore, in the section beginning with, "having attained the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana)," the meaning should be understood thus: "having attained the state of the sphere of infinite space."

The rest is evident.
90
90. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, so attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘‘natthi kiñcī’’ti ākiñcaññāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho , bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī’’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.
90.
“To him another says: ‘Indeed, sir, there is such a self (ātman) as you assert. I do not deny that it doesn't exist; but that self is not completely annihilated merely by that.
For there is, good sir, another self belonging to the base of nothingness, completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness: “There is nothing” (natthi kiñcī).
You do not know it or see it.
But I know it and see it.
Since this self, good sir, is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body (kāyassa bhedā) and does not exist after death, at this point the self (ātman) is completely annihilated."
In this way some proclaim the annihilation (ucchedaṃ), destruction (vināsaṃ), and extermination (vibhavaṃ) of an existent being (sato sattassa).
88-92.Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagotiādīsu pana ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaṃ upagatoti, evamattho veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.
88-92. The meaning of "completely transcending all perceptions of form ( rūpasaññā)," and so on, is explained in the Visuddhimagga.
Moreover, in the phrases beginning with "having attained the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana)," the meaning should be understood thus: "he has attained the state of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-bhavaṃ upagato)."
The rest here is evident.
91
91. ‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hoti. Atthi kho, bho, añño attā sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘‘santametaṃ paṇītameta’’nti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpago. Taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi. Tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. So kho, bho, attā yato kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti.
91. Another says to him: “Sir, there is such a self (ātman) as you say; I do not say that this self does not exist; but that self is not completely annihilated at this point.

For there is, good sir, another self (ātman) that, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana), enters the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), thinking, "This is peaceful; this is sublime."

That you neither know nor see.

But I know it and see it.

It is this self (ātman) that, with the breakup of the body (kāya), is annihilated and destroyed, and does not exist after death; it is in this way that the self (ātman) is completely annihilated."

In this way, some proclaim the annihilation (uccheda), destruction (vināsa), and non-existence (vibhava) of an existing being (satta).
88-92.Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagotiādīsu pana ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaṃ upagatoti, evamattho veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.
88-92. The meaning of "completely transcending all perceptions of form," and so on, is explained in the Visuddhimagga.

Furthermore, in "[one] has attained the sphere of the infinity of space," and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: "[one] has attained existence in the sphere of the infinity of space."

The rest is clear.
92
92. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā ucchedavādā sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti sattahi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ucchedavādā sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti, sabbe te imeheva sattahi vatthūhi…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
92. "It is on these grounds, monks, that those ascetics and Brahmins who are annihilationists ( ucchedavādā ) proclaim the annihilation ( ucchedaṃ ), destruction ( vināsaṃ ), and extermination ( vibhavaṃ ) of an existent being ( sato sattassa ) in seven ways.

Whatever recluses or Brahmins proclaim the annihilation ( ucchedaṃ ), destruction ( vināsaṃ ), and extermination ( vibhavaṃ ) of an existent being ( sato sattassa ), all of them do so on these seven grounds... and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak.
88-92.Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagotiādīsu pana ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaṃ upagatoti, evamattho veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.
88-92. The meaning of the fourth, namely, the complete transcending of perceptions of form ( sarvaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkama), etc., is explained in the Visuddhimagga.

Moreover, regarding, "one who has attained the ākāsānañcāyatana," etc. (ākāsānañcāyatanūpagotiādīsu), the meaning should be understood thus: "he has attained the state of the ākāsānañcāyatana (ākāsānañcāyatanabhavaṃ upagato)."

The rest here is evident.
93
93. ‘‘Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti pañcahi vatthūhi. Te ca bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kimāgamma kimārabbha diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti pañcahi vatthūhi?
93. "There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins who are proclaimers of dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna Here and Now), and who proclaim supreme dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna here and now) for an existent being in five ways.

And upon what grounds, based on what, do those venerable ascetics and Brahmins, proclaimers of dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna Here and Now), proclaim supreme dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna here and now) for an existent being in five ways?
93. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāde diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkhadhammo vuccati, tattha tattha paṭiladdhattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhamme nibbānaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, imasmiṃyeva attabhāve dukkhavūpasamananti attho. Taṃ vadantīti diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā. Paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānanti paramaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ uttamanti attho.
93. In the doctrine of diṭṭhadhammanibbāna, diṭṭhadhamma is called directly experienced dhamma. This is a designation for the individuality obtained in this or that state of existence. Diṭṭhadhamme nibbānaṃ, diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, means the subsiding of suffering in this very individuality. Those who say that are the proponents of the diṭṭhadhammanibbāna doctrine. Paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ means the highest diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, the ultimate.
94
94. ‘‘Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘‘yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.
94.

"Here, monks, some ascetic or brāhmaṇa holds such a view and proclaims such a doctrine: 'When this self (attā), good sir, is furnished and replete with the five strands of sense pleasures (pañcahi kāmaguṇehi), and indulges in them, at that very point, good sir, this self (attā) attains the supreme Nirvāṇa (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ) here and now!'"

In this way, some proclaim the highest Nirvāṇa attainable in this very life (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ) for an existent being.
94.Pañcahi kāmaguṇehīti manāpiyarūpādīhi pañcahi kāmakoṭṭhāsehi bandhanehi vā. Samappitoti suṭṭhu appito allīno hutvā. Samaṅgībhūtoti samannāgato. Paricāretīti tesu kāmaguṇesu yathāsukhaṃ indriyāni cāreti sañcāreti itocito ca upaneti. Atha vā laḷati ramati kīḷati. Ettha ca duvidhā kāmaguṇā – mānusakā ceva dibbā ca. Mānusakā mandhātukāmaguṇasadisā daṭṭhabbā, dibbā paranimmitavasavattidevarājassa kāmaguṇasadisāti. Evarūpe kāme upagatānañhi te diṭṭhadhammanibbānasampattiṃ paññapenti.
94. "With the five strands of sense pleasure": that is, with the five desirable sense-fields such as pleasant forms, which are like sensual attachments or bonds.

"Devoted to": being well and truly devoted, having become absorbed.

"Endowed with": being furnished with.

“Revels”: he allows his sense faculties to roam and wander among those strands of sense pleasure according to his wish, indulging in them in this way and that.

Or else: he sports, delights, and plays with them.

The strands of sense pleasure (kāmaguṇā) are twofold, the human (mānusakā) and the divine (dibbā).

The human are to be regarded as like the sense pleasures of King Mandhātu; the divine are like the sense pleasures of the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.

The theorists proclaim the achievement of nirvāṇa here and now only for those who have acquired such sense pleasures (kāme).
95
95. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha –‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Kāmā hi, bho, aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, tesaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Yato kho , bho, ayaṃ attā vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.
95.
“Then another says to him: ‘There is, good sir, such a self (ātman) as you assert. That I do not deny. But it is not at that point that the self (ātman) attains supreme nibbāna here and now.

What is the reason for that? Because, good sir, sense pleasures (kāmā) are impermanent (aniccā), suffering (dukkha), subject to change (vipariṇāmadhammā), and through their change and transformation there arise sorrow (soka), lamentation (parideva), pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and despair (upāyāsā).

But when this self (ātman), quite secluded from sense pleasures (kāmehi), secluded from unwholesome states (akusalehi dhammehi), enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial thought (savitakka) and sustained thought (savicāra) and contains the rapture and happiness (pītisukhaṃ) born of seclusion (vivekajaṃ)—at this point, good sir, the self (ātman) attains supreme nibbāna here and now.’

In this way, some proclaim supreme nibbāna here and now for an existent being.
95. Dutiyavāre hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā paṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhā, pakatijahanaṭṭhena vipariṇāmadhammāti veditabbā. Tesaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvāti tesaṃ kāmānaṃ vipariṇāmasaṅkhātā aññathābhāvā, yampi me ahosi, tampi me natthīti vuttanayena uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Tattha antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇo soko, tannissitalālappanalakkhaṇo paridevo, kāyappaṭipīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, manovighātalakkhaṇaṃ domanassaṃ, visādalakkhaṇo upāyāso, vivicceva kāmehītiādīnamattho visuddhimagge vutto.
95. Having occurred for the second time, they should be understood as impermanent due to the characteristic of absence (abhāvaṭṭhena), as suffering (duḥkha) due to the characteristic of oppression (paṭipīḷanaṭṭhena), and as subject to transformation (vipariṇāmadhamma) due to the characteristic of abandoning their original nature (pakatijahanaṭṭhena).

Their transformation is otherness: the otherness consisting of the transformation of those desires. "What I had, that I no longer have" - in accordance with this previously stated method, sorrow (śoka), lamentation (parideva), suffering (duḥkha), displeasure (domanassa), and despair (upāyāsa) arise.

There, sorrow (śoka) has the characteristic of inward contemplation (antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇo); lamentation (paridevo) has the characteristic of compulsive talking based on that (tannissitalālappanalakkhaṇo); suffering (duḥkha) has the characteristic of bodily oppression (kāyappaṭipīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ); displeasure (daumanassaṃ) has the characteristic of mental agitation (manovighātalakkhaṇaṃ); despair (upāyāso) has the characteristic of dejection (visādalakkhaṇo). The meaning of "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (vivicceva kāmehītiādi) and so forth is stated in the Visuddhimagga.
96
96. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yadeva tattha vitakkitaṃ vicāritaṃ, etenetaṃ oḷārikaṃ akkhāyati. Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.
96. Another says to him: ‘There is, sir, such a self (ātmā) as you assert; I do not say that there is not. But it is not at this point that the self attains the supreme Nirvāṇa here and now (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hoti).

Why is that? Because that jhāna contains initial thought (vitakkitaṃ) and sustained thought (vicāritaṃ); therefore it is declared to be gross (oḷārikaṃ akkhāyati).

But when, sir, the self, by the subsiding of initial and sustained thought (vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā), enters and abides in the second jhāna (dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ), which has inner tranquility (ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ) and oneness of mind (cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ), is without initial thought (avitakkaṃ) and sustained thought (avicāraṃ), and contains the rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukhaṃ) born of concentration (samādhijaṃ), that is when the self realises the supreme Nirvāṇa here and now (paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hoti)."

In this way, some proclaim the supreme Nirvāṇa here and now for an existent being (satassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti).
96.Vitakkitanti abhiniropanavasena pavatto vitakko. Vicāritanti anumajjanavasena pavatto vicāro. Etenetanti etena vitakkitena ca vicāritena ca etaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ oḷārikaṃ sakaṇḍakaṃ viya khāyati.
96. Thinking (vitakka) is the thought that occurs through focusing the mind. Consideration (vicāra) is the reflection that occurs through sustained application. Because of this, the first dhyāna (paṭhamajjhānaṃ), with its thinking and consideration, appears coarse (oḷārikaṃ), like something with husks (sakaṇḍakaṃ).
97
97. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yadeva tattha pītigataṃ cetaso uppilāvitattaṃ, etenetaṃ oḷārikaṃ akkhāyati. Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti ‘‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’’ti, tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.
97. Another says to him: ‘Sir, there is such a self ( attā) as you say. I don’t deny it. But that is not when the self attains the supreme Nibbāna here and now.

Why is that? It is declared to be gross because of the mental exhilaration (uppilāvitattaṃ) connected with rapture (pīti) that exists there.

But when the self, with the fading away of rapture (pītiyā virāgā), one abides in equanimity (upekkhako), mindful (sato) and clearly comprehending (sampajāno), and still experiencing happiness (sukhaṃ) with the body (kāyena), enters and abides in the third jhāna, so that the ariyas announce: “He abides happily (sukhavihārī), in equanimity (upekkhako) and mindfulness (satimā)”—at this point, good sir, the self attains supreme Nibbāna here and now.’

That is how some proclaim the highest Nibbāna here and now for an existent being.
97-98.Pītigatanti pītiyeva. Cetaso uppilāvitattanti cittassa uppilabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Cetaso ābhogoti jhānā vuṭṭhāya tasmiṃ sukhe punappunaṃ cittassa ābhogo manasikāro samannāhāroti. Sesamettha diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāde uttānameva. Ettāvatā sabbāpi dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo kathitā honti. Yāsaṃ satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo.
97-98.
Pīti means just pīti.
The elated state of consciousness means the act of making consciousness elated.
The application of consciousness means, having arisen from jhāna, the application of consciousness, attention (manasikāra), and directing the mind (samannāhāra) again and again towards that bliss.
The rest is evident in the discourse on nirvāṇa visible in this very life (dṛṣṭadharm નિર્વાણavāda).
At this point, all sixty-two views have been explained.
Seven of these views belong to annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi), the remainder to eternalism (śāśvatadṛṣṭi).
98
98. ‘‘Tamañño evamāha – ‘atthi kho, bho, eso attā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, neso natthīti vadāmi; no ca kho, bho, ayaṃ attā ettāvatā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yadeva tattha sukhamiti cetaso ābhogo, etenetaṃ oḷārikaṃ akkhāyati. Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ patto hotī’ti. Ittheke sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti.
98. Another says to him: “Sir, there is such a self (ātman) as you say. I do not deny it. But it is not at that point that the self (ātman) attains the supreme Nirvāṇa here and now.

Why is that? Because the mind contains the idea of joy there, and that state is considered gross (oḷārika).

But when, good sir, this self (ātman), with the abandonment of pleasure (sukha) and pain (duḥkha), with the disappearance of previous joy (saumanasya) and grief (daurmanasya), enters and abides in the fourth jhāna, which is without pleasure and pain and contains purification of mindfulness through equanimity (upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ)—at this point, good sir, this self (ātman) attains supreme Nirvāṇa here and now.”

In this way some proclaim the supreme Nirvāṇa here and now for an existent being.
97-98.Pītigatanti pītiyeva. Cetaso uppilāvitattanti cittassa uppilabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Cetaso ābhogoti jhānā vuṭṭhāya tasmiṃ sukhe punappunaṃ cittassa ābhogo manasikāro samannāhāroti. Sesamettha diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāde uttānameva. Ettāvatā sabbāpi dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo kathitā honti. Yāsaṃ satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo.
97-98.
pītigati means just pīti (joy, rapture).
Cetaso uppilāvitatta means cittassa uppilabhāvakaraṇaṃ: making consciousness buoyant.
Cetaso ābhogo means, having arisen from jhāna (meditative absorption), the repeated application, attention (manasikāra), and directing (samannāhāra) of the mind to that happiness (sukha).
The rest in the explanation of the dṛṣṭadharma nirvāṇa vāda (the doctrine of nirvāṇa in this very life) is but clear.
At this point, all the sixty-two views (dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhi) have been explained.
Of these, seven are annihilationist views (ucchedadiṭṭhi), and the rest are eternalist views (sassatadiṭṭhi).
99
99. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti pañcahi vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā sato sattassa paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññapenti, sabbe te imeheva pañcahi vatthūhi…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
"It is through these five grounds, monks, that those ascetics and Brahmins who advocate a doctrine of dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna here and now) propound the supreme dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna here and now) for an existing being.

Whatever ascetics or Brahmins, monks, are proponents of dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna here and now), and propound the supreme dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa (Nibbāna here and now) for an existing being, all of them do so only through these five grounds…and… those who would rightly speak of the Tathāgata's true qualities would speak of these."
100
100. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā aparantakappikā aparantānudiṭṭhino aparantaṃ ārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti catucattārīsāya vatthūhi. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā aparantakappikā aparantānudiṭṭhino aparantaṃ ārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti, sabbe te imeheva catucattārīsāya vatthūhi…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
“It is on these forty-four grounds, monks, that those ascetics and Brahmins who are speculators about the future ( aparantakappikā), who hold settled views about the future (aparantānudiṭṭhino), assert various conceptual theorems (adhimuttipadāni) referring to the future.

Whatever ascetics or Brahmins, monks, are speculators about the future (aparantakappikā), hold settled views about the future (aparantānudiṭṭhino), and assert various conceptual theorems (adhimuttipadāni) referring to the future, all of them do so on these very forty-four grounds…and it is concerning these that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak.
100-104. Idāni – ‘‘imehi kho te, bhikkhave’’ti iminā vārena sabbepi te aparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Puna – ‘‘imehi, kho te bhikkhave’’tiādinā vārena sabbepi te pubbantāparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā tadeva ñāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Iti ‘‘katame ca te, bhikkhave, dhammā’’tiādimhi pucchamānopi sabbaññutaññāṇameva pucchitvā vissajjamānopi sattānaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ tulāya tulayanto viya sinerupādato vālukaṃ uddharanto viya dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni uddharitvā sabbaññutaññāṇameva vissajjeti. Evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā. Tayo hi suttassa anusandhī – pucchānusandhi, ajjhāsayānusandhi, yathānusandhīti. Tattha ‘‘evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – kiṃ nu kho, bhante, orimaṃ tīraṃ, kiṃ pārimaṃ tīraṃ, ko majjhe saṃsīdo, ko thale ussādo, ko manussaggāho, ko amanussaggāho, ko āvaṭṭaggāho, ko antopūtibhāvo’’ti (saṃ. ni. 4.241) evaṃ pucchantānaṃ bhagavatā vissajjitasuttavasena pucchānusandhi veditabbo. Atha kho aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…, vedanā…, saññā…, saṅkhārā …, viññāṇaṃ anattā, anattakatāni kira kammāni kamattānaṃ phusissantī’’ti. Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā ceto parivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṃ atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya – ‘‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…pe… phusissantī’’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.10). Evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavatā vuttasuttavasena ajjhāsayānusandhi veditabbo. Yena pana dhammena ādimhi desanā uṭṭhitā, tassa dhammassa anurūpadhammavasena vā paṭipakkhavasena vā yesu suttesu upari desanā āgacchati, tesaṃ vasena yathānusandhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasutte heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari cha abhiññā āgatā. Vatthasutte heṭṭhā kilesena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari brahmavihārā āgatā. Kosambakasutte heṭṭhā bhaṇḍanena uṭṭhitā, upari sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā. Kakacūpame heṭṭhā akkhantiyā uṭṭhitā, upari kakacūpamā āgatā. Imasmimpi brahmajāle heṭṭhā diṭṭhivasena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari suññatāpakāsanaṃ āgataṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā’’ti.
100-104.
Now, collecting into one all the speculators about the future in the section beginning “it is on these grounds, bhikkhus (monks)” , he reveals his knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).

And again, collecting into one all the speculators about the past and the future in the section beginning “it is on these grounds, bhikkhus (monks)” , he again reveals this same knowledge (ñāṇa).

Thus, when in the beginning he asked: “And what, bhikkhus (monks), are those dhammas that are deep, etc.? ”, he asked only in reference to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). And answering this question, the Exalted One answers by means of the same knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), bringing forth the sixty-two speculative views (diṭṭhigatāni) just as if he were weighing the inclinations (ajjhāsayaṃ) of beings with a pair of scales or removing the sand from the foot of Mount Sineru.

Thus, this teaching (desanā) has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure (yathānusandhi) of the teaching.

For suttas have three kinds of sequence of meaning (anusandhi): a sequence of meaning based on a question (pucchānusandhi): a sequence of meaning dictated by inclination (ajjhāsayānusandhi); and a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure (yathānusandhi).

Herein, the “sequence of meaning based on a question” (pucchānusandhi) can be understood through those suttas the Exalted One pronounced in response to those who questioned him, as the following passage illustrates: “When this was said, a certain bhikkhu (monk) said to the Exalted One: ‘What, Lord (bhante), is the lower shore (orimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is the further shore (pārimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is sinking in the middle (majjhe saṃsīdo)? What is being thrown up on dry land (thale ussādo)? What is seizure by humans (manussaggāho), by non-humans (amanussaggāho) and by a whirlpool (āvaṭṭaggāho)? What is inner putridity (antopūtibhāvo)? “ (Saṃ.
Ni.
4.
241)

Then, in the mind (cetaso) of a certain bhikkhu (monk) this thought (parivitakko) arose: “So, it seems, material form (rūpaṃ) is not self (anattā), feeling (vedanā) is not self (anattā), perception (saññā) is not self (anattā), formations (saṅkhārā) are not self (anattā), consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) is not self (anattā). What self (kamattānaṃ), then, will actions (kammāni) done by the not-self (anattakatāni) affect?”

Then the Blessed One (bhagavā), knowing with his mind (cetasā) the thought in the mind (ceto) of that bhikkhu (monk), addressed the bhikkhus (monks) thus: “It is possible (ṭhānaṃ), bhikkhus (monks), that some misguided man (moghapuriso) here, obtuse (avidvā) and ignorant (avijjāgato), with his mind (cetasā) dominated by craving (taṇhādhipateyyena) might think that he can outstrip (atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya) the Teacher’s Dispensation (satthusāsanaṃ) thus: ‘So, it seems, material form (rūpaṃ) is not self (anattā)… what self (phusissantī)?”

“What do you think (maññatha), bhikkhus (monks), is material form (rūpaṃ) permanent (niccaṃ) or impermanent (aniccaṃ)?” (Ma. Ni. 3. 10).

Thus, having understood the inclinations (ajjhāsayaṃ) of others, the “sequence of meaning dictated by inclination” (ajjhāsayānusandhi) can be understood through those suttas (vuttasuttavasena) the Exalted One pronounced (bhagavatā).

The “sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching” (yathānusandhi) can be understood through those suttas in which the teaching (desanā) progresses from its initial subject to its culmination by way of counterparts (anurūpadhamma), or by way of the opposites (paṭipakkha) of the initial subject.

For example, in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta the teaching (desanā) is set up at the beginning by way of virtue (sīlena) and culminates in the six kinds of direct knowledge (cha abhiññā).

In the Vattha Sutta, the teaching (desanā) is set up by way of the defilements (kilesena) and culminates in the sublime abodes (brahmavihārā).

In the Kosambiya Sutta, the teaching (desanā) is set up by way of schism (bhaṇḍanena) and culminates in the principles of fraternal harmony (sāraṇīyadhammā).

In the Kakacūpama, the teaching (desanā) is set up at the beginning by way of patience (akkhantiyā) and culminates in the Kakacūpama.

And in this Brahmajāla Sutta, the teaching (desanā) is set up at the beginning by way of views (diṭṭhivasena) and culminates in the elucidation of emptiness (suññatāpakāsanaṃ).

Thus it is said: “This teaching (desanā) has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure (yathānusandhivasena) of the teaching.
101
101. ‘‘Imehi kho te, bhikkhave, samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbantakappikā ca aparantakappikā ca pubbantāparantakappikā ca pubbantāparantānudiṭṭhino pubbantāparantaṃ ārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti dvāsaṭṭhiyā vatthūhi.
“It is on these sixty-two grounds, monks, that those ascetics and Brahmins who are speculators about the past ( pubbantakappikā), speculators about the future (aparantakappikā), and speculators about the past and the future together (pubbantāparantakappikā), who hold settled views about the past and the future (pubbantāparantānudiṭṭhino), assert various conceptual theorems (adhimuttipadāni) referring to the past and the future (pubbantāparantaṃ ārabbha).
100-104. Idāni – ‘‘imehi kho te, bhikkhave’’ti iminā vārena sabbepi te aparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Puna – ‘‘imehi, kho te bhikkhave’’tiādinā vārena sabbepi te pubbantāparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā tadeva ñāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Atha kho aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…, vedanā…, saññā…, saṅkhārā …, viññāṇaṃ anattā, anattakatāni kira kammāni kamattānaṃ phusissantī’’ti. Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā ceto parivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṃ atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya – ‘‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…pe… phusissantī’’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.10). Evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavatā vuttasuttavasena ajjhāsayānusandhi veditabbo. Yena pana dhammena ādimhi desanā uṭṭhitā, tassa dhammassa anurūpadhammavasena vā paṭipakkhavasena vā yesu suttesu upari desanā āgacchati, tesaṃ vasena yathānusandhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasutte heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari cha abhiññā āgatā. Vatthasutte heṭṭhā kilesena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari brahmavihārā āgatā. Kosambakasutte heṭṭhā bhaṇḍanena uṭṭhitā, upari sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā. Kakacūpame heṭṭhā akkhantiyā uṭṭhitā, upari kakacūpamā āgatā. Imasmimpi brahmajāle heṭṭhā diṭṭhivasena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari suññatāpakāsanaṃ āgataṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā’’ti.
100-104.

Now, collecting into one all the speculators about the future in the section beginning “it is on these grounds,” the Exalted One reveals his knowledge of omniscience ( sabbaññutaññāṇa).

And collecting into one all the speculators about the past and the future in the section beginning “it is on these grounds,” he again reveals this same knowledge.

Thus, when in the beginning he asked: “And what, bhikkhus, are those dharmas?,” he asked only in reference to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). And answering this question, the Exalted One answers by means of the same knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), bringing forth the sixty-two speculative views just as if he were weighing the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of beings with a pair of scales or removing the sand from the foot of Mount Sineru.

This teaching has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhi).

For suttas have three kinds of sequence of meaning: a sequence of meaning based on a question (pucchānusandhi), a sequence of meaning dictated by inclination (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhi).

Herein, the “sequence of meaning based on a question (pucchānusandhi)” is found in those suttas the Exalted One pronounced in response to those who questioned him, as the following passage illustrates: “When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Exalted One: ‘What, Bhante, is the lower shore (orimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is the further shore (pārimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is sinking in the middle (majjhe saṃsīdo)? What is being thrown up on dry land (thale ussādo)? What is seizure by humans (manussaggāho), by non-humans (amanussaggāho) and by a whirlpool (āvaṭṭaggāho)? What is inner putridity (antopūtibhāvo)?’”.

Thus, when questioned, the Blessed One answered by way of suttas, and this is called question-based connection.

Then the following line of thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: “It is said that material form (rūpa) is not-self (anattā), feeling (vedanā) is not-self (anattā), perception (saññā) is not-self (anattā), mental formations (saṅkhārā) are not-self (anattā), consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) is non-self (anattā). What self, then, do kammas done without a self affect?”

Then the Exalted One, discerning with his mind the thought in this bhikkhu’s mind, addressed the bhikkhus: “It is possible, bhikkhus, that a certain foolish man here, confused, immersed in ignorance and dominated by craving, may imagine in his mind that he can overshoot the dispensation of the Master, thus: ‘It is said that material form (rūpa) is non-self (anattā)’ etc.."

“What do you think, bhikkhus, is material form (rūpa) permanent (niccaṃ) or impermanent (aniccaṃ)?”

The “sequence of meaning dictated by inclination (ajjhāsayānusandhi)” can be understood through those suttas the Exalted One pronounced after he had understood the inclinations (ajjhāsayaṃ) of others.

The “sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhi)” can be understood through those suttas in which the teaching progresses from its initial subject to its culmination by way of counterparts or by way of the opposites of the initial subject.

For example, in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta the teaching is set up at the beginning by way of virtue (sīla) and culminates in the six kinds of direct knowledge (abhiññā).

In the Vattha Sutta, the teaching is set up by way of the defilements (kilesa) and culminates in the sublime abodes (brahmavihārā).

In the Kosambiya Sutta, the teaching is set up by way of schism (bhaṇḍana) and culminates in the principles of fraternal harmony (sāraṇīyadhammā).

In the Kakacūpama, the teaching is set up at the beginning by way of patience (akkhanti) and culminates in the Kakacūpama.

And in this Brahmajāla Sutta, the teaching is set up at the beginning by way of views (diṭṭhi) and culminates in the elucidation of emptiness (suññatāpakāsanaṃ).

Thus it is said: “This teaching has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhi).”
102
102. ‘‘Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā pubbantakappikā vā aparantakappikā vā pubbantāparantakappikā vā pubbantāparantānudiṭṭhino pubbantāparantaṃ ārabbha anekavihitāni adhimuttipadāni abhivadanti, sabbe te imeheva dvāsaṭṭhiyā vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena; natthi ito bahiddhā.
“Whatever ascetics or brāhmaṇas, bhikkhus, are speculators about the past (pūrvānta), or speculators about the future (aparānta), or speculators about the past and the future together (pūrvāntāparānta), hold settled views about the past and the future, and assert various conceptual theorems referring to the past and the future, all of them do so on these sixty-two grounds or on a certain one of them. Outside of these there is none.
100-104. Idāni – ‘‘imehi kho te, bhikkhave’’ti iminā vārena sabbepi te aparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Puna – ‘‘imehi, kho te bhikkhave’’tiādinā vārena sabbepi te pubbantāparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā tadeva ñāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Iti ‘‘katame ca te, bhikkhave, dhammā’’tiādimhi pucchamānopi sabbaññutaññāṇameva pucchitvā vissajjamānopi sattānaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ tulāya tulayanto viya sinerupādato vālukaṃ uddharanto viya dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni uddharitvā sabbaññutaññāṇameva vissajjeti. Evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā. Tayo hi suttassa anusandhī – pucchānusandhi, ajjhāsayānusandhi, yathānusandhīti. Tattha ‘‘evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – kiṃ nu kho, bhante, orimaṃ tīraṃ, kiṃ pārimaṃ tīraṃ, ko majjhe saṃsīdo, ko thale ussādo, ko manussaggāho, ko amanussaggāho, ko āvaṭṭaggāho, ko antopūtibhāvo’’ti (saṃ. ni. 4.241) evaṃ pucchantānaṃ bhagavatā vissajjitasuttavasena pucchānusandhi veditabbo. Atha kho aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…, vedanā…, saññā…, saṅkhārā …, viññāṇaṃ anattā, anattakatāni kira kammāni kamattānaṃ phusissantī’’ti. Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā ceto parivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṃ atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya – ‘‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…pe… phusissantī’’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.10). Evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavatā vuttasuttavasena ajjhāsayānusandhi veditabbo. Yena pana dhammena ādimhi desanā uṭṭhitā, tassa dhammassa anurūpadhammavasena vā paṭipakkhavasena vā yesu suttesu upari desanā āgacchati, tesaṃ vasena yathānusandhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasutte heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari cha abhiññā āgatā. Vatthasutte heṭṭhā kilesena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari brahmavihārā āgatā. Kosambakasutte heṭṭhā bhaṇḍanena uṭṭhitā, upari sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā. Kakacūpame heṭṭhā akkhantiyā uṭṭhitā, upari kakacūpamā āgatā. Imasmimpi brahmajāle heṭṭhā diṭṭhivasena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari suññatāpakāsanaṃ āgataṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā’’ti.
100-104.
Now, collecting into one all the speculators about the future in the section beginning “it is on these grounds, monks,” the Exalted One reveals his knowledge of omniscience ( sabbaññutaññāṇa).
And again, collecting into one all the speculators about the past and the future in the section beginning “it is on these grounds, monks,” he again reveals this same knowledge ( ñāṇa).
Thus, when in the beginning he asked: “And what, monks, are those dharmas?,” he asked only in reference to the knowledge of omniscience ( sabbaññutaññāṇa). And answering this question, the Exalted One answers by means of the same knowledge of omniscience, bringing forth the sixty-two speculative views ( diṭṭhigata ) just as if he were weighing the inclinations ( ajjhāsaya ) of beings with a pair of scales or removing the sand from the foot of Mount Sineru.

This teaching has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhi).
For suttas have three kinds of sequence of meaning ( anusandhi): a sequence of meaning based on a question ( pucchānusandhi), a sequence of meaning dictated by inclination ( ajjhāsayānusandhi), and a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching ( yathānusandhi).
Herein, the “sequence of meaning based on a question” is found in those suttas the Exalted One pronounced in response to those who questioned him, as the following passage illustrates: “When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Exalted One: ‘What, Lord (bhante), is the lower shore ( orimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is the further shore ( pārimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is sinking in the middle ( majjhe saṃsīdo)? What is being thrown up on dry land ( thale ussādo)? What is seizure by humans ( manussaggāho), by non-humans ( amanussaggāho) and by a whirlpool ( avaṭṭaggāho)? What is inner putridity ( antopūtibhāvo)?’”
Thus, when he was asked a question, the pucchānusandhi should be understood, by way of the Blessed One's suttas in response to questions.
Then the following line of thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: “It is said, sir ( bho), that material form ( rūpaṃ ) is not-self ( anattā), feeling ( vedanā ) is not-self, perception ( saññā ) is not-self, mental formations ( saṅkhārā ) are not-self, consciousness ( viññāṇaṃ ) is non-self ( anattā). What self, then, do kammas done without a self affect?”
Then the Exalted One, discerning with his mind this bhikkhu's thought, addressed the bhikkhus: “It is possible, monks ( bhikkhave), that a certain foolish man ( moghapuriso ) here, confused ( avidvā), immersed in ignorance ( avijjāgato ) and dominated by craving ( taṇhādhipateyyena ) , may imagine in his mind that he can overshoot the dispensation of the Master (satthusāsanaṃ ), thus: ‘“It is said, sir ( bho ), that material form (rūpaṃ) is non-self (anattā)… etc. … what self will actions affect?’”
“What do you think, bhikkhus, is material form (rūpaṃ) permanent ( niccaṃ) or impermanent (aniccaṃ)?”

Thus, the “sequence of meaning dictated by inclination” (ajjhāsayānusandhi) can be understood through those suttas the Exalted One pronounced after he had understood the inclinations ( ajjhāsaya ) of others.
The “sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching” (yathānusandhi) can be understood through those suttas in which the teaching progresses from its initial subject to its culmination by way of counterparts or by way of the opposites of the initial subject, by whichever dharma the teaching started in the beginning.
For example, in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta the teaching is set up at the beginning by way of virtue ( sīla) and culminates in the six kinds of direct knowledge (abhiññā).
In the Vattha Sutta, the teaching is set up by way of the defilements ( kilesa ) and culminates in the sublime abodes ( brahmavihārā).
In the Kosambiya Sutta, the teaching is set up by way of schism ( bhaṇḍana) and culminates in the principles of fraternal harmony ( sāraṇīyadhammā).
In the Kakacūpama, the teaching is set up at the beginning by way of patience ( akkhanti) and culminates in the Kakacūpama.
And in this Brahmajāla Sutta, the teaching is set up at the beginning by way of views (diṭṭhi) and culminates in the elucidation of emptiness ( suññatāpakāsanaṃ).
Thus it is said: “This teaching has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching ( yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā ).”
103
103. ‘‘Tayidaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato pajānāti – ‘ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃgahitā evaṃparāmaṭṭhā evaṃgatikā bhavanti evaṃabhisamparāyā’ti. Tañca tathāgato pajānāti, tato ca uttaritaraṃ pajānāti, tañca pajānanaṃ na parāmasati, aparāmasato cassa paccattaññeva nibbuti viditā. Vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto, bhikkhave, tathāgato.
"This, monks, the Tathāgata understands: 'These viewpoints, thus grasped and thus adhered to, will lead to such and such destinations in another world.' (ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃgahitā evaṃparāmaṭṭhā evaṃgatikā bhavanti evaṃabhisamparāyā'ti).

The Tathāgata understands this, and even more than this, but he is not attached to that knowledge. And because he is free from misapprehension, he has realized within himself perfect peace (nibbuti).

Having understood as they really are the arising (samudaya) and passing away (atthaṅgama) of feelings (vedanānaṃ), their satisfaction (assāda), their unsatisfactoriness (ādīnava), and the escape (nissaraṇa) from them, the Tathāgata, monks, is liberated through non-clinging (anupādāvimutto)."
100-104. Idāni – ‘‘imehi kho te, bhikkhave’’ti iminā vārena sabbepi te aparantakappike ekajjhaṃ niyyātetvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ vissajjeti. Seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasutte heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari cha abhiññā āgatā. Vatthasutte heṭṭhā kilesena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari brahmavihārā āgatā. 100-104.

Now, collecting into one all the speculators about the future in the section beginning "it is on these grounds, bhikkhus," the Exalted One reveals his knowledge of omniscience.

And again, collecting into one all the speculators about the past and the future in the section beginning "it is on these grounds, bhikkhus," he reveals this same knowledge.

Thus, when in the beginning he asked: “And what, bhikkhus, are those dharmas that are deep, etc.?”, he asked only in reference to the knowledge of omniscience. And answering this question, the Exalted One answers by means of the same knowledge of omniscience, bringing forth the sixty-two speculative views just as if he were weighing the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of beings with a pair of scales or removing the sand from the foot of Mount Sineru.

Ni.

241) Thus, the sequence of meaning based on a question (pucchānusandhi) can be understood through those suttas the Blessed One pronounced in response to those who questioned him.

Then the following line of thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: ‘It is said, sir, that material form (rūpa) is not-self (anattā), feeling (vedanā) is not-self, perception (saññā) is not-self, mental formations (saṅkhārā) are not-self, consciousness (viññāṇa) is not-self. Ni.

10).

104. ‘‘Ime kho te, bhikkhave, dhammā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā santā paṇītā atakkāvacarā nipuṇā paṇḍitavedanīyā, ye tathāgato sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti, yehi tathāgatassa yathābhuccaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ.
“These, monks, are those dharmas that are profound (gambhīra), difficult to see (duddasa), difficult to understand (duranubodha), peaceful (santa), excellent (paṇīta), beyond the realm of logic (atakkāvacara), subtle (nipuṇa), and to be experienced by the wise (paṇḍitavedanīya), which the Tathāgata having realized them himself with direct knowledge (abhiññā sacchikatvā), proclaims; and it is concerning these qualities that those who would rightly praise the Tathāgata in accordance with reality would speak.

Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā ceto parivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati, yaṃ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṃ atidhāvitabbaṃ maññeyya – ‘‘iti kira bho rūpaṃ anattā…pe… phusissantī’’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.10). Evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavatā vuttasuttavasena ajjhāsayānusandhi veditabbo. Yena pana dhammena ādimhi desanā uṭṭhitā, tassa dhammassa anurūpadhammavasena vā paṭipakkhavasena vā yesu suttesu upari desanā āgacchati, tesaṃ vasena yathānusandhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasutte heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari cha abhiññā āgatā. Vatthasutte heṭṭhā kilesena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari brahmavihārā āgatā. Kosambakasutte heṭṭhā bhaṇḍanena uṭṭhitā, upari sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā. Kakacūpame heṭṭhā akkhantiyā uṭṭhitā, upari kakacūpamā āgatā. Imasmimpi brahmajāle heṭṭhā diṭṭhivasena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari suññatāpakāsanaṃ āgataṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘evamayaṃ yathānusandhivasena desanā āgatā’’ti.
100-104.
Now, collecting into one all those who speculate about the future in the section beginning "it is on these grounds, monks," the Exalted One reveals his knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ).
And again, collecting into one all those who speculate about the past and the future in the section beginning "it is on these grounds, monks," he reveals this same knowledge.
Thus, when in the beginning he asked: "And what, monks, are those dharmas?", he asked only in reference to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ). And answering this question, the Exalted One answers by means of the same knowledge of omniscience, bringing forth the sixty-two speculative views (dvāsatthi ditthigatāni) just as if he were weighing the inclinations (ajjhāsayam) of beings with a pair of scales or removing the sand from the foot of Mount Sineru.
Thus, this teaching (desanā) has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhivasena).
For suttas have three kinds of sequence of meaning: a sequence of meaning based on a question (pucchānusandhi), a sequence of meaning dictated by inclination (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhi).
Herein, the "sequence of meaning based on a question" is found in those suttas the Exalted One pronounced in response to those who questioned him, as the following passage illustrates: "When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Exalted One: 'What, Lord (bhante), is the lower shore (orimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is the further shore (pārimaṃ tīraṃ)? What is sinking in the middle (majjhe saṃsīdo)? What is being thrown up on dry land (thale ussādo)? What is seizure by humans (manussaggāho), by non-humans (amanussaggāho) and by a whirlpool (āvaṭṭaggāho)? What is inner putridity (antopūtibhāvo)?'"
Thus, when questioned, the sequence of meaning based on a question should be understood through the Blessed One's discourse in response to the question.
Then the following line of thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: "It is said, sir (bho), that form (rūpaṃ) is not-self (anattā), feeling (vedanā) is not-self, perception (saññā) is not-self, mental formations (saṅkhārā) are not-self, consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) is non-self (anattā). What self, then, do kammas done without a self affect?"
Then the Exalted One, discerning with his mind this bhikkhu's thought, addressed the bhikkhus: "It is possible, bhikkhus, that a certain foolish man (moghapuriso) here, confused (avidvā), immersed in ignorance (avijjāgato) and dominated by craving (taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā), may imagine in his mind that he can overshoot the dispensation (satthusāsanaṃ) of the Master, thus: 'It is said, sir (bho), that material form (rūpaṃ) is non self (anattā)…etc… what will [actions] affect?'"
“What do you think, bhikkhus, is material form (rūpaṃ) permanent (niccaṃ) or impermanent (aniccaṃ)?”
Thus, having understood the inclinations (ajjhāsayaṃ) of others, the sequence of meaning dictated by inclination should be understood through those suttas the Exalted One pronounced.
The “sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching” can be understood through those suttas in which the teaching (desanā) progresses from its initial subject to its culmination by way of counterparts (anurūpadhammavasena) or by way of the opposites (paṭipakkhavasena) of the initial subject.
For example, in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta the teaching (desanā) is set up at the beginning by way of virtue (sīlena) and culminates in the six kinds of direct knowledge (cha abhiññā āgatā).
In the Vattha Sutta, the teaching (desanā) is set up by way of the defilements (kilesena) and culminates in the sublime abodes (brahmavihārā āgatā).
In the Kosambiya Sutta, the teaching (desanā) is set up by way of schism (bhaṇḍanena) and culminates in the principles of fraternal harmony (sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā).
In the Kakacūpama [Sutta], the teaching (desanā) is set up at the beginning by way of patience (akkhantiyā) and culminates in the Kakacūpama.
And in this Brahmajāla Sutta, the teaching (desanā) is set up at the beginning by way of views (ditthivasena) and culminates in the elucidation of emptiness (suññatāpakāsanaṃ āgataṃ).
Thus, it is said: “This teaching (desanā) has come down by way of a sequence of meaning dictated by the natural structure of the teaching (yathānusandhivasena)."
105
105. ‘‘Tatra, bhikkhave, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā sassatavādā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi , tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva.
"Therein, monks, those ascetics and Brahmins who are proponents of the eternalist doctrine, propound the self (ātman) and the world as eternal based on four grounds; that is merely the feeling of those ascetics and Brahmins who do not know and do not see, and is merely the agitation and vacillation of those immersed in craving (tṛṣṇā)."
105-117. Idāni mariyādavibhāgadassanatthaṃ – ‘‘tatra bhikkhave’’tiādikā desanā āraddhā. Tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditamevāti yena diṭṭhiassādena diṭṭhisukhena diṭṭhivedayitena te somanassajātā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavantānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ kevalaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃyeva taṃ vedayitaṃ, tañca kho panetaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva. Diṭṭhisaṅkhātena ceva taṇhāsaṅkhātena ca paritassitena vipphanditameva calitameva kampitameva thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇusadisaṃ, na sotāpannassa dassanamiva niccalanti dasseti. Esa nayo ekaccasassatavādādīsupi.
105-117.
Now, in order to show the distinction of boundaries, the teaching beginning with “tatra bhikkhave (there, monks)” is undertaken.

Furthermore, that feeling of those ascetics and brāhmaṇas who do not know or see, who are attached to craving, is agitation and vacillation. Because of the satisfaction of views (dṛṣṭi-āsvāda), the pleasure of views (dṛṣṭi-sukha), and the feeling of views (dṛṣṭi-vedayita), they, being born of joy (saumanasya-jātā), proclaim the self (ātman) and the world to be eternal (śāśvata) on four grounds. Furthermore, that feeling of those ascetics and brāhmaṇas who do not know or see the true nature (sabhāva) of phenomena (dhamma) as it really is (yathābhūta), who are attached to craving, indeed, that feeling is only of those attached to craving, and that is only agitation and vacillation.

Designated by view (dṛṣṭi-saṅkhāta) and designated by craving (tṛṣṇā-saṅkhāta), agitated and vacillating, it is only trembling, only shaking, only quivering, like a stake (khāṇu) planted in a heap of chaff (thusarāśi); it does not show unshakability like the vision (darśana) of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

The same method (naya) applies to the eternalist theories (ekacca-śāśvata-vāda) and so on.
106
106. ‘‘Tatra, bhikkhave, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā ekaccasassatikā ekaccaasassatikā ekaccaṃ sassataṃ ekaccaṃ asassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva.
“There, monks, when those ascetics and Brahmins who are partly eternalists (ekaccasassatikā) and partly non-eternalists (ekaccaasassatikā) proclaim the self (attānam) and the world (lokam) to be partly eternal (sassataṃ) and partly non-eternal (asassataṃ) on four grounds, that too is only the feeling of those ascetics and Brahmins who do not know (ajānataṃ) and do not see (apassataṃ); that is only the agitation (paritassita) and vacillation (vipphandita) of those who are immersed in craving (taṇhāgatānaṃ).
105-117. Idāni mariyādavibhāgadassanatthaṃ – ‘‘tatra bhikkhave’’tiādikā desanā āraddhā. Tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditamevāti yena diṭṭhiassādena diṭṭhisukhena diṭṭhivedayitena te somanassajātā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavantānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ kevalaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃyeva taṃ vedayitaṃ, tañca kho panetaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva. Diṭṭhisaṅkhātena ceva taṇhāsaṅkhātena ca paritassitena vipphanditameva calitameva kampitameva thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇusadisaṃ, na sotāpannassa dassanamiva niccalanti dasseti. Esa nayo ekaccasassatavādādīsupi.
105-117.
Now, in order to show the distinction of boundaries, the teaching beginning with "There, monks..." is undertaken.

Even that feeling of those ascetics and Brahmins who do not know, do not see, who are attached to craving is only agitation and vacillation; the satisfaction of views ( dṛṣṭi-āsvāda), the pleasure of views ( dṛṣṭi-sukha), the feeling of views ( dṛṣṭi-vedayita), on account of which they, being born of joy, proclaim the self ( ātman) and the world ( loka) to be eternal ( śāśvata) on four grounds; even that is only the feeling of those ascetics and Brahmins who do not know and do not see the true nature ( svabhāva) of phenomena ( dhamma) as it really is ( yathābhūta); it is only the feeling of those who are entirely immersed in craving, and that is only agitation and vacillation.

Designated by view ( dṛṣṭi-saṃkhāta) and also designated by craving ( tṛṣṇā-saṃkhāta), agitated by craving, it is only agitation and vacillation, it is only trembling, it is only shaking, like a stake planted in a heap of chaff; it does not show the unshakable vision like that of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

The same method ( naya) applies to the eternalist views ( ekacca-śāśvata-vāda) and so on.
107
107. ‘‘Tatra , bhikkhave, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā antānantikā antānantaṃ lokassa paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva.
107. "There, monks, those ascetics and Brahmins who are Finitists and Infinitists, propounding the finitude and infinitude of the world (lokassa) on four grounds, that is merely the feeling of those ascetics and Brahmins who do not know (ajānataṃ) and do not see (apassataṃ), the agitation and vacillation of those who are immersed in craving (taṇhāgatānaṃ)."
105-117. Idāni mariyādavibhāgadassanatthaṃ – ‘‘tatra bhikkhave’’tiādikā desanā āraddhā. Tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditamevāti yena diṭṭhiassādena diṭṭhisukhena diṭṭhivedayitena te somanassajātā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavantānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ kevalaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃyeva taṃ vedayitaṃ, tañca kho panetaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva. Diṭṭhisaṅkhātena ceva taṇhāsaṅkhātena ca paritassitena vipphanditameva calitameva kampitameva thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇusadisaṃ, na sotāpannassa dassanamiva niccalanti dasseti. Esa nayo ekaccasassatavādādīsupi.
105-117. Now, in order to show the demarcation of boundaries, the teaching beginning with "Tatra Bhikkhave (there, monks)" is undertaken.

Even that feeling of those esteemed ascetics and Brahmins who do not know, do not see, and are immersed in craving, that agitation and vacillation by which, through the satisfaction of views (dṛṣṭi-āsvāda), the pleasure of views (dṛṣṭi-sukha), and the feeling of views (dṛṣṭi-vedayita), they, being filled with joy, proclaim the self (ātman) and the world to be eternal (śāśvata) on four grounds; even that is only the feeling of those esteemed ascetics and Brahmins who do not know and do not see the true nature (sabhāva) of phenomena (dhamma) as it really is (yathābhūta); it is only the feeling of those who are entirely immersed in craving. And that is only agitation and vacillation.

Agitation and vacillation, caused by what is reckoned as views (dṛṣṭi-saṅkhāta) and what is reckoned as craving (taṇhā-saṅkhāta) and is agitated, is just wavering, just shaking, just trembling, like a stake planted in a heap of chaff; it is not unshakable like the vision (darśana) of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

The same method applies to the eternalist theory (ekaccasassatavāda) and so on.
108
108. ‘‘Tatra, bhikkhave, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā amarāvikkhepikā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭhā samānā vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjanti amarāvikkhepaṃ catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva.
108.
"And furthermore, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brāhmaṇas who are endless equivocators, when questioned on this and that point, resort to evasive statements and endless equivocation on four grounds; that is merely the agitated trembling of those ascetics and brāhmaṇas who do not know, do not see, are subject to feeling, and are driven by craving (tṛṣṇā)."
105-117. Idāni mariyādavibhāgadassanatthaṃ – ‘‘tatra bhikkhave’’tiādikā desanā āraddhā. Tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ajānataṃ apassataṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditamevāti yena diṭṭhiassādena diṭṭhisukhena diṭṭhivedayitena te somanassajātā sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti catūhi vatthūhi, tadapi tesaṃ bhavantānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ vedayitaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃ kevalaṃ taṇhāgatānaṃyeva taṃ vedayitaṃ, tañca kho panetaṃ paritassitavipphanditameva. Diṭṭhisaṅkhātena ceva taṇhāsaṅkhātena ca paritassitena vipphanditameva calitameva kampitameva thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇusadisaṃ, na sotāpannassa dassanamiva niccalanti dasseti.
